Fp G-module can be written as an N-linear combination of modules in X inside the
Grothendieck group of Fp G?
    The “only if” direction is proved, and the affirmative answer is obtained if p does
not divide |G| (D. Johnston, D. Rumynin, J. Algebra, 687, no. 1 (2026), 776–791).
                                                               D. Johnston, D. Rumynin

21.61. For a fixed (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there
an algorithm that, given a finite subset S of G, finds a finite presentation for the
subgroup H = ⟨S⟩? Cf. 4.8 in Archive.                                    I. Kapovich

21.62. Is the uniform subgroup membership problem decidable for (finitely generated
free)-by-cyclic groups? That is, for a fixed group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm
that, given elements w, h1 , . . . , hk ∈ G, decides whether or not w belongs to the
subgroup H = ⟨h1 , . . . , hk ⟩?                                          I. Kapovich
                           New Problems (21st issue, 2026)                               177

21.63. (E. Zelmanov). Let F be a field of characteristic p > 0, and let Γ be the
principal congruence subgroup of Aut(F [x1 , . . . , xn ]) consisting of all automorphisms
that send each variable xi to xi modulo terms of higher degree. Then Γ is a residually-
p group. Does Γ satisfy a pro-p identity?                                      E. I. Khukhro

21.64. Is it true that if a normal subgroup A of a Sylow p-subgroup of a p-soluble
finite group G has exponent pe , then the normal closure of A in G has (p, e)-bounded
(or even e-bounded) p-length?                                           E. I. Khukhro

21.65. Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G. Must G
contain a subgroup of index bounded in terms of |φ| and |CG (φ)| whose Fitting
height is bounded
   (a) in terms of |φ|?
   (b) or even in terms of the composition length of ⟨φ⟩?
    An affirmative answer to part (b) is known when |φ| is a prime power (B. Hartley–
V. Turau), or when (|G|, |φ|) = 1 (A. Turull, B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs). Also cf. 19.43.
                                                                             E. I. Khukhro

21.66. Suppose that A is a nilpotent group of automorphisms of a finite soluble group
G. Is the Fitting height of G bounded in terms of |A| and |CG (A)|?
    An affirmative answer is known when (|G|, |A|) = 1 (J. G. Thompson, even for
soluble A, with improved bounds in subsequent papers of H. Kurzweil, A. Turull,
B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs), when A is cyclic (see 19.43), or when CG (A) = 1 (E. C. Dade).
Note that for any non-nilpotent finite group A there are finite soluble groups G of
unbounded Fitting height with CG (A) = 1 (S. D. Bell–B. Hartley).         E. I. Khukhro

21.67. Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G, and let r
be the (Prüfer) rank of the fixed-point subgroup CG (φ). Is the Fitting height of G
bounded terms of |φ| and r?
   This is known to be true in the case where |φ| is a product of at most two prime
powers (B. Hartley, Preprint, 1994, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.
com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/hartley94-prepr-mims.pdf). An affirmative
answer to this question would imply an affirmative answer to 13.8(b). E. I. Khukhro


21.68. A finite group G is said to be semi-abelian if it has a sequence of subgroups
1 = G0 ⩽ G1 ⩽ · · · ⩽ Gn = G such that for every i the subgroup Gi+1 is isomorphic
to a quotient of a semidirect product Ai ⋊ Gi for some abelian group Ai .
    Conjecture: Semi-abelian finite groups are monomial.                     M. Kida

21.69. Is there an algorithm deciding if a given one-relator group is hyperbolic?
                                                                                  D. Kielak

21.70. A group G is called an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension n over
a ring R if it is of type FP over R and Hi (G; RG) = 0 for i ̸= n, while Hn (G; RG) = R
as an RG-module, where the action on R is trivial. (Note that G is not required to
be finitely presented.) If G is an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension n
over all fields, is it an orientable Poincaré duality group over the integers? D. Kielak
 178                          New Problems (21st issue, 2026)

21.71. For a ring R, we say that a group G is of type FL(R) if the trivial RG-module
R admits a finite resolution by finitely generated free modules. If R is a field, we
define the Euler characteristic of G over R to be the alternating sum of R-ranks of
homology groups Hi (G; R).
    Does there exist a group of type FL(Fi ) for two fields F1 and F2 such that the
Euler characteristics of the group over the fields F1 and F2 differ?        D. Kielak

21.72. We say that a group is a Tarski monster if it is finitely generated, not cyclic,
and all of its proper non-trivial subgroups are isomorphic to each other.
   a) Do there exist amenable torsion-free Tarski monsters?
   b) Do there exist amenable Tarski monsters of prime exponent?             D. Kielak

21.73. Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable?
   See the definition of CT(Z) in 17.57.                                         S. Kohl

21.74. Is it algorithmically decidable whether a given element g ∈ CT(Z)
  (a) permutes a nontrivial partition of Z into residue classes?
  (b) has only finite cycles?
  (c) has no finite cycles?                                                      S. Kohl

21.75. Given two distinct sets P1 and P2 of odd primes none of which is a subset of
the other, is it true that ⟨CTP1 (Z), CTP2 (Z)⟩ ⪇ CTP1 ∪P2 (Z)?
   See the definition of CTP (Z) in 17.60.                                  S. Kohl

21.76. Let σ = (σij ), 1 ⩽ i ̸= j ⩽ n, be an irreducible elementary net (carpet)
of order n ⩾ 3 over a field K (see 19.48). The net σ is said to be closed if the
elementary net subgroup E(σ) does not contain new elementary transvections. The
net σ is said to be completable if its diagonal can be supplemented with subgroups
to a complete net. Completable elementary nets are closed. It is known that over
fields of characteristic 0 and 2 there exist irreducible closed elementary nets that are
not completable (V. A. Koibaev, Trudy Inst. Mat. Mekh. Ural Div. Ross. Akad.
Nauk, 17, no. 4 (2011), 134–141 (Russian); V. A. Koibaev, Siberian Math. J., 62,
no. 2 (2021), 262–266).
    Do there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order n ⩾ 3 over a field of odd
characteristic that are not completable?                                  V. A. Koibaev

21.77. Let d be an integer that is not divisible√by n-th powers of primes, let xn − d
be an irreducible polynomial over Q, let θ = n d, and let K = Q(θ) be the radical
extension of degree n of the field Q. The multiplicative group K ∗ of the field K is
canonically embedded into the group AutQ (K) of all invertible Q-linear mappings of
the Q-space K; let T be the image of K ∗ under this embedding. In the natural basis
1, θ, θ2 , . . . , θn−1 of the Q-space K the group AutQ (K) corresponds to G = GL(n, Q),
and the subgroup T to a subgroup T (d) (unsplit maximal torus). Every subgroup H
of G containing T (d) and some one-dimensional transformation is rich in elementary
transvections (V. A. Koibaev, St. Petersbg. Math. J., 21, no. 5 (2010), 731–742)
and thus defines a net σ = σ(H) (V. A. Koibaev, A. V. Shilov, J. Math. Sci. New
York 171, no. 3 (2010), 380–385). Let E(σ) denote the subgroup generated by all
transvections in the net group G(σ). Is it true that H ⩽ NG (E(σ))?
    This inclusion was proved in the case n = 2 (V. A. Koibaev, Dokl. Math., 41, no. 3
(1990), 414–416).                                                           V. A. Koibaev
                            New Problems (21st issue, 2026)                                179

21.78. Let p be a prime and let G be a pro-p group. Suppose that all of the
(continuous Galois) cohomology groups H n (G, Fp ) of G with coefficients in the field
of p elements are finite. Does it necessarily follow that the cohomology ring H ∗ (G, Fp )
is finitely generated?
     The answer is known to be ‘yes’ if G is abelian-by-(p-adic analytic), as follows
from (J. King, Commun. Algebra, 27, no. 10 (1999), 4969–4991).             P. Kropholler



21.79. Let G be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set S and
the corresponding word metric LS (∗). An element g is said to be distorted in G if
LS (g n )/n → 0 as n → ∞; this notion is independent of the choice of the generating
set S. For any, not necessarily finitely generated, group H, an element g ∈ H is said
to be distorted if there is a finitely generated subgroup G of H containing g in which
g is distorted. Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups in which every
nontrivial element is distorted?
    Note that it is straightforward to construct countable (not finitely generated) left-
orderable groups with this property using HN N -extensions and applying results of
V. V. Bludov and A. M. W. Glass.                                     Y. Lodha, A. Navas



21.80. Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups with only one nontrivial
conjugacy class?
   A positive answer to this question implies a positive answer to 21.78. Note that
D. Osin constructed torsion-free finitely generated groups with only one nontrivial
conjugacy class; see 9.10 in Archive.                              Y. Lodha, A. Navas



21.81. (J. Wiegold). Let Γ be a finite simple group and let Nn (Γ) denote the set of
normal subgroups of the free group Fn of rank n whose quotient is isomorphic to Γ.
   Conjecture: Aut(Fn ) acts transitively on Nn (Γ) for n ⩾ 3.
   This is not true for n = 2 (B. H. Neumann, H. Neumann, Math. Nachr., 4 (1951),
106–125).                                                              A. Lubotzky



21.82. Conjecture: For n ⩾ 3, there are no finite simple characteristic quotients of
the free group Fn .
   This is not true for n = 2 (W. Y. Chen, A. Lubotzky, P. H. Tiep, to appear in
Comment. Math. Helvetici, 2025).                                        A. Lubotzky



21.83. The function dn (σ, τ ) = (1/n)·|{x ∈ {1, . . . , n} | σ(x) ̸= τ (x)}| is a distance on
the symmetric group Sn . For a finitely generated group G, an almost-homomorphism
is a sequence of set-theoretic maps fn : G → Sn satisfying dn (fn (g)fn (h), fn (gh)) → 0
as n → ∞ for all g, h ∈ G. An almost-homomorphism {fn } is said to be close to a
homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms ρn : G → Sn such that
dn (ρn (g), fn (g)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g ∈ G. The group G is said to be permutation
stable if every almost-homomorphism of G is close to a homomorphism.
    Conjecture: Metabelian groups are permutation-stable.                        A. Lubotzky
 180                           New Problems (21st issue, 2026)

                                                                              A. Lubotzky

21.86. (M. Gromov, B. Weiss). A group G is said to be sofic if for every finite set
F ⊆ G containing 1 and every ε > 0 there exist n ∈ N and a map φ : F → Sn such
that φ(1) = 1, d(φ(gh), φ(g)φ(h)) < ε for all g, h such that gh ∈ F , φ(g) does not

21.90. Let Γ be a graph of diameter d. For i ∈ {1, 2, . . . , d}, let Γi be the graph on
the same vertex set as Γ with vertices u, w adjacent in Γi if and only if dΓ (u, w) = i.
Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that Γ2
and Γ3 are strongly regular?                                              A. A. Makhnëv

21.91. (W. Willems). Conjecture: The sum of squares of the degrees of the irreducible
p-Brauer characters of a finite group G is at least the p′ -part of |G|.
    This is known to be true for p = 2 (G. Malle, Adv. Math., 380 (2021), Paper
no. 107609, 15 pp.).                                                         G. Malle
                            New Problems (21st issue, 2026)                                 181

21.92. Conjecture: The number of irreducible p-Brauer characters of a finite group
G is bounded above by the maximum of the number of conjugacy classes k(H) in
p′ -subgroups H of G.                           G. Malle, G. Navarro, G. Robinson


21.93. (M. Herzog, J. Schönheim). Let G be a group and let k ⩾ 2. Let H1 , . . . , Hk
be subgroups of G, and g1 , . . . , gk elements of G such that the cosets g1 H1 , . . . , gk Hk
form a partition of G. Is it true that |G : Hi | = |G : Hj | for some i ̸= j?

baum, A. Fraenkel, Fund. Math., 128, no. 3 (1987), 139–144). Also cf. 20.99.
                                                                                  L. Margolis


21.94. The Gruenberg–Kegel graph (or the prime graph) GK(G) of a finite group G
is a labelled graph with vertex set consisting of all prime divisors of the order of G in
which different vertices p and q are adjacent if and only if G contains an element of
order pq. Let GK(G) denote the abstract graph obtained from GK(G) by removing
all labels. A finite group G is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its
Gruenberg–Kegel graph if there are no finite groups H ∼   ̸ G with GK(H) isomorphic
                                                           =
to GK(G).
    Are there infinitely many (pairwise non-isomorphic) finite groups which are recog-
nizable by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph?              N. V. Maslova

21.95. Is there an almost simple but not simple group which is recognizable by the
isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph?

Kegel graph, then G is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, and therefore G
is almost simple (P. J. Cameron, N. V. Maslova, J. Algebra, 607 (2022), 186–213).
                                                                               N. V. Maslova

21.96. Is it true that a periodic group containing an involution is locally finite if the
centralizer of every element of even order is locally finite?           V. D. Mazurov

∗ 21.97. (M. Tărnăuceanu). Is it true that for every positive rational number r there
exists a finite group G such that | Aut(G)|/|G| = r?

and posets (R. Molinier, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21059). It
is also known that the set {| Aut(G)|/|G| | G is a finite abelian group} is dense in
[0, +∞) (M. Tărnăuceanu, Elemente Math. (2025), https://ems.press/journals/
em/articles/14298544).                                                     R. Molinier
  ∗ Yes, it is true (S. Sureaux, Preprint, 2026, https://kourovkanotebookorg.
wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/21.97-solution.pdf).

the set of w-values is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups. Is it true that the
verbal subgroup w(G) is finite-by-cyclic?
   This is true for lower central words (G. Cutolo, C. Nicotera, J. Algebra, 324, no. 7
(2010), 1616–1624).                                                          M. Morigi

21.99. Conjecture: If G is a transitive permutation group on a finite set Ω, then for
any distinct α, β in Ω there is an element g ∈ G with αg = β whose number of fixed
points is different from 1.                                                 P. Müller

automorphisms. Let C = CG (A) be the fixed-point subgroup, and let C ′ denote its
derived subgroup.
    Is it true that the number of A-invariant irreducible characters χ of G whose
restriction χC is never zero is exactly |C/C ′ |? This would follow if one could show
that χC is never zero if and only if the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondent χ∗ of χ is
linear.                                                                    G. Navarro

21.101. Which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of regular
polytopes of rank 3? In other words, which finite almost simple groups are generated
by three involutions two of which commute?
   This question has been answered for finite simple groups; see 7.30 in Archive.
                                                                                   Ya. N. Nuzhin


21.102. Let V be a variety generated by a finite group, and let f (n)p be the order
of the free group in V on n generators. Is it true that the sequence n log f (n) has a
limit as n → ∞, and this limit is an integer?                       A. Yu. Olshanskii


21.103. (V. V. Uspenskii). A Hausdorff topological group G is called minimal if it
does not admit a strictly coarser Hausdorff group topology. A topological group is
called Raikov complete if its two-sided uniform structure is complete. It is known
that a finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups is again
minimal. Is it true that an arbitrary Cartesian product of Raikov complete minimal
topological groups remains minimal?
    It is known that an arbitrary Cartesian product of centre-free minimal topological
groups is minimal (M. Megrelishvili, Topology Appl., 62, no. 1 (1995), 1–19). D. Peng

such that em (x1 , . . . , xn ) = 1.

(see 15.12) satisfies the iterated identity w, then G is a torsion group.

Alcober, M. Noce, G. Tracey, J. Algebra, 554 (2020), 54–77).                           M. Petschick

every group G in C such that the set Gw of word values of w in G is finite, the verbal
subgroup w(G) = ⟨Gw ⟩ is also finite (see also Archive 2.45). Is every word concise in
the class of residually finite groups?
   See (D. Segal, Words. Notes on verbal width in groups, Cambridge Univ. Press,
2009) for a partial solution.                                            M. Petschick

said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set

finite (cf. 21.105 and Archive 2.45). Is every formula with one free variable concise
in the class of residually finite groups?                               M. Petschick

called expansive if for every open subset U there is a number m such that Fn ∩ U ̸= ∅
for all n > m. Suppose that a countable group G can be partitioned into countably
many dense subsets. Is it true that in G there exists an expansive sequence? Cf. 15.80.

codegrees of G (see 20.78). Define σ(G) = max{|π(m)| : m ∈ Cod(G)}, where π(m)
denotes the set of prime divisors of an integer m. It is proved that there exists
a constant k such that |π(G)| ⩽ k · σ(G) for every finite group G (Y. Yang, G. Qian,
J. Algebra, 478 (2017), 215–219), but the estimate provided for k is very crude. Can
the constant k be taken as 4?                                                G. Qian




21.109. Conjecture: The derived length of a finite solvable group G does not exceed
|Cod(G)| − 1.
   The Fitting height of G is known to be at most min{|Cod(G)|−1, |Cod(G)|/2+1}
(G. Qian, Y. Zeng, J. Group Theory, to appear).                             G. Qian

phism of S. Let α(x) be the smallest number of conjugates of x in G = ⟨x, Inn S⟩
that generate G. The values of α(x) had been studied in (R. Guralnick, J. Saxl, J.
Algebra, 268, no. 2 (2003), 519–571).
   (a) (R. Guralnick, J. Saxl). Conjecture: If S is an exceptional group of Lie type,
then α(x) ⩽ 5 for every nonidentity automorphism x of S.
  (b) For each exceptional group S of Lie type, find the largest value of α(x).
                                                                           D. O. Revin

2

conjugates of x in ⟨x, Inn(S)⟩ generate a subgroup of order not divisible by 3. If S
admits a τ -automorphism, we call S a τ -group.
   (a) List all τ -groups up to isomorphism.
   (b) Do τ -automorphisms of odd order exist?                 D. O. Revin, N. Y. Yang

taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. The symmetric boundary of
a complete class X other than the class of all finite groups is defined as the largest
integer n such that Sn ∈ X. Every positive integer n ̸= 3 coincides with the symmetric
boundary of some complete class. It is proved (mod CFSG, D. O. Revin, Algebra i
Analiz, 37, no. 1 (2025), 141–176 (Russian)) that, for every complete class X, there
exists a nonnegative integer m with the following property: for every finite group

symmetric boundary n.

of G which vanishes on all p-singular elements of G and whose value at each p-regular
element x of G is the number of p-elements of CG (x).
    (a) Is it true that Ψp,G is a character of G?
    (b) If yes, can Ψp,G be afforded by a projective RG-module, where R is a complete

a splitting field for G and its subgroups, and the residue field R/J(R) is a splitting
field of characteristic p for G and its subgroups?
     It is known that Ψp,G is a character when G ∼  = Sn for any positive integer n and
any prime p (T. Scharf, J. Algebra, 139, no. 2 (1991), 446–457).            G. Robinson



21.114. A finite group G is called weakly ab-maximal if |H : [H, H]| ⩽ |G : [G, G]|
for all H ⩽ G. Do weakly ab-maximal groups have bounded derived length?
    It is known that weakly ab-maximal groups are direct products of weakly ab-
maximal p-groups (F. Lisi, L. Sabatini, J. Group Theory, 27 (2024), 1203–1217).
                                                                               L. Sabatini

I found information about Scharf's 1991 paper on the root number function in symmetric groups. T. Scharf's "Die Wurzelanzahlfunktion in symmetrischen Gruppen" was published in Journal of Algebra, volume 139 (1991), pages 446-457.

The search results show that this work relates to the root number function in symmetric groups, which concerns counting solutions to equations like x^n = g in symmetric groups. The m-th root number function of S_n is a sum of higher Lie characters and hence is itself a character - a result due to Scharf. This indicates the paper establishes a connection between root number functions and character theory of symmetric groups.

The work deals with statistical aspects of symmetric groups, asymptotic properties of (ordinary) characters of symmetric groups, and estimates for the multiplicities of root number functions.

# Problem 21.32 (P. J. Cameron) — "Is G the derived subgroup of some finite group?" is decidable

**Problem 21.32.** Is the following problem decidable, and if so, what is its complexity? Given a finite
group G, is there a finite group H such that the derived subgroup of H is isomorphic to G?

**Answer.** Yes, it is decidable. More precisely:

> **Theorem A.** Let G be a finite group, let e = 2·exp(Z(G)), and let m = ⌈log₂|G|⌉. If G ≅ H′ for some
> finite group H, then G ≅ (H*)′ for a finite group H* with
>
>   |H*| ≤ |Aut(G)| · |Z(G)|² · e^{2m}.
>
> Consequently the problem is decidable (search all groups of order at most this bound), and the bound is
> quasi-polynomial in |G| (since |Aut(G)| ≤ |G|^{log₂|G|}); so the problem lies in NTIME(n^{O(log n)}) for
> input size n = |G| (a witness H* of quasi-polynomial size, on which "H*′ ≅ G" is checked in quasi-polynomial
> time).

> **Theorem B (necessary condition; sufficient when Z(G)=1).** If G ≅ H′ for a finite group H, then there is a
> subgroup Q with Inn(G) ≤ Q ≤ Aut(G) and Q′ = Inn(G). If Z(G) = 1 the converse holds: G ≅ H′ for some finite
> H if and only if Inn(G) ≅ G is the derived subgroup of some subgroup Q of Aut(G) containing Inn(G).
> In particular, for centerless G the problem reduces to a finite computation inside Aut(G).

Examples: S₃ and D₈ are not derived subgroups of any finite group (Theorem B: Aut(S₃)=S₃ has derived
subgroup C₃ ≠ Inn(S₃); Aut(D₈) = D₈ has no subgroup Q ⊇ Inn(D₈) ≅ C₂² with Q′ = C₂²), while Q₈ = SL(2,3)′
and A₄ = S₄′. (These examples are confirmed by brute force in `work/p21_32/`.)

## 1. Set-up and the basic structure

Throughout, H is a finite group with H′ = G (we identify G with the subgroup H′ ≤ H). Put

  K := C_H(G),  Z := Z(G).

(1.1) H/G is abelian (as G = H′).
(1.2) K ⊴ H and H/K embeds in Aut(G) (conjugation action). Its image Q := H/K contains Inn(G) = GK/K.
(1.3) K ∩ G = C_G(G) = Z.
(1.4) [H, K] ≤ H′ ∩ K = G ∩ K = Z (using K ⊴ H). In particular K′ ≤ Z, so K is nilpotent of class ≤ 2, and
      K/Z is central in H/Z. Also K ≤ C_H(Z) since K centralises G ⊇ Z.
(1.5) Commutator calculus: for h,h′ ∈ H and k,k′ ∈ K,
        [hk, h′k′] = [h,h′k′]^k [k,h′k′] = ([h,k′][h,h′]^{k′})^k · [k,k′][k,h′]^{k′}.
      The factors [h,k′], [k,h′], [k,k′] lie in Z ≤ K, and Z is centralised by K. Hence, for any subgroup
      H₁ ≤ H with H = H₁K, one has
        G = H′ = H₁′ · [H₁,K] · K′,                                             (∗)
      where the right-hand side is a subgroup because [H₁,K]K′ ≤ Z ≤ G ≤ H₁ normalises H₁′ and H₁′ ≤ G
      is centralised by K.

**Proof of Theorem B.** Put H̃ = H/Z, K̃ = K/Z, G̃ = G/Z. By (1.4) K̃ is central in H̃, and H̃/K̃ ≅ H/K = Q.
Since H′ = G we get H̃′ = G̃, and G̃ ∩ K̃ = (G ∩ K)/Z = 1 by (1.3). The projection π: H̃ → Q maps H̃′ onto
Q′ with kernel H̃′ ∩ K̃ = G̃ ∩ K̃ = 1, so π restricts to an isomorphism G̃ = H̃′ → Q′; but π(G̃) = π(GK/K) is
precisely the group Inn(G) of inner automorphisms. Hence Q′ = Inn(G).
If Z(G) = 1 then K ∩ G = 1, [H,K] = 1, so K ≤ Z(H) and H′ ∩ K = 1; hence H′ ≅ (H/K)′ = Q′ = Inn(G) ≅ G is
realised by the subgroup Q ≤ Aut(G) itself (take H := Q). ∎

## 2. Reduction 1: bounded rank

Since G = H′ is generated by commutators [a,b] (a,b ∈ H) and every generating set of a group of order |G|
contains a generating subset of size ≤ log₂|G|, we can choose a₁,b₁,…,a_m,b_m ∈ H, m ≤ log₂|G|, with
G = ⟨[a_i,b_i] : i ≤ m⟩. Let H₀ := ⟨G, a₁,b₁,…,a_m,b_m⟩. Then H₀′ ⊇ ⟨[a_i,b_i]⟩ = G and H₀′ ≤ H′ = G, so
H₀′ = G. Moreover H₀/G is an abelian group generated by the 2m images of the a_i, b_i.
Replacing H by H₀ we may and do assume:

central extension 1 → M → E → Q → 1 with class η:

      "Hopf map" h_η : H₂(Q) → M equals M ∩ E′.

>

>
> Consequently the problem is decidable (search all groups of order at most this bound), and the bound is
> quasi-polynomial in |G| (since |Aut(G)| ≤ |G|^{log₂|G|}); so the problem lies in NTIME(n^{O(log n)}) for
> input size n = |G| (a witness H* of quasi-polynomial size, on which "H*′ ≅ G" is checked in quasi-polynomial
> time).

> **Theorem B (necessary condition; sufficient when Z(G)=1).** If G ≅ H′ for a finite group H, then there is a
> subgroup Q with Inn(G) ≤ Q ≤ Aut(G) and Q′ = Inn(G). If Z(G) = 1 the converse holds: G ≅ H′ for some finite
> H if and only if Inn(G) ≅ G is the derived subgroup of some subgroup Q of Aut(G) containing Inn(G).
> In particular, for centerless G the problem reduces to a finite computation inside Aut(G).

subgroup C₃ ≠ Inn(S₃); Aut(D₈) = D₈ has no subgroup Q ⊇ Inn(D₈) ≅ C₂² with Q′ = C₂²), while Q₈ = SL(2,3)′
and A₄ = S₄′. (These examples are confirmed by brute force in `work/p21_32/`.)

Sambale, B., and Tǎrnǎuceanu, M. published "On the size of coset unions" in the Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics, volume 55, pages 979–987 (2022).

Based on the search results, here's what I found about derived subgroups (commutator subgroups) of finite groups:

## Definition and Basic Properties

The commutator subgroup (also called a derived group) of a group G is the subgroup generated by the commutators of its elements. It is the unique smallest normal subgroup such that the quotient is Abelian.

## Which Finite Groups Are Derived Subgroups?

Two important cases describe which groups can serve as derived subgroups:

1. **Abelian groups**: Derived subgroup is trivial if and only if group is abelian.

2. **Perfect groups**: A group which equals its own commutator subgroup is termed a perfect group.

## Key Examples

The search results provide specific examples:
- The commutator subgroup of the symmetric group is the alternating group, and the commutator subgroup of the alternating group is the whole group.
- In the quaternion group with eight elements, the commutators form the subgroup.

## Additional Research Areas

Research on derived subgroups includes studying their structural properties. For instance, the derived subgroup of a finite group is nilpotent if and only if certain conditions on primary commutators hold, and iterating the commutator subgroup-defining function produces the derived series, and groups whose derived series terminates at the identity in finitely many steps are termed solvable groups.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the concepts you're inquiring about:

## Root Number Function and Higher Frobenius-Schur Indicators

Higher indicators (with m > 2) arise when one considers the root number function in a finite group, which assigns to a group element the number of its m-th roots—the number of group elements whose m-th power equals the given element.

## Classical Frobenius-Schur Indicator

For the standard indicator (m = 2), the Frobenius-Schur indicator of a character χ is defined as 0 if χ is not real-valued, 1 if the representation is defined over ℝ, and -1 if χ is real-valued but the representation is not defined over ℝ.

A classical result connects this to counting roots: The number of elements v in G such that v² = g equals the sum over all irreducible characters χ of ε(χ)χ(g), where ε(χ) is the Frobenius-Schur indicator.

## Prime Power Orders and Character Theory

The Frobenius-Schur indicators are invariant under the action of the Galois group (making them rational), and as algebraic integers, this proves that higher Frobenius-Schur indicators are integers in the case of group rings.

These results show how the root number function generalizes the classical Frobenius-Schur indicator theory to higher m-th roots in finite groups.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

<result># Kourovka Notebook, Issues 1–9 (lines 138–1592): computationally tractable open problems

Lines 138–1592 of `/project/docs/21tkt.txt` were read in full. Problems marked solved (∗ with "Yes/No/proved" comments: 2.48, 3.46, 5.47, 5.52, 6.30, 6.45, 8.11, 8.51, 8.75, 9.41c, 9.42, 9.66, 9.69) were excluded. Most of the remaining ~200 problems are about infinite/ordered/topological/varietal groups and were de-prioritised. Below are the candidates worth a 1–2-day attack, ranked by score.

## Score 4

**8.44** (lines 1206–1211, J. Mennicke). Groups G_p = ⟨a,b | a²=b^p=(ab)³=(b^r a b^{−2r} a)²=1⟩ with r²+1≡0 (mod p). Prove/disprove that G_p is infinite for all but finitely many p; known finite for p ≤ 17 (by computer).
Plan: first open cases p = 29, 37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97. In GAP: coset enumeration (ACE package, large tables) for finiteness; for infiniteness use `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup` + `AbelianInvariants` (a finite-index subgroup with infinite abelianisation), or KBMAG/`IsHyperbolic` (kbmag/walrus) since G_p is a one-relator quotient of the hyperbolic (2,3,p) triangle group; curvature/small-cancellation arguments (Edjvet–Howie style) could then give the "all but finitely many" statement. Score 4 — a direct computation settles each new p; the general statement is plausible with known one-relator-quotient techniques.

**2.78 + 3.57** (lines 292–303 and 411–412, P. I. Trofimov). An "IEn̄-system" of a finite G is the set of all subgroups of a given order containing a non-normal one; k is "soluble" if every group with exactly k systems is soluble, "simple/absolutely simple/composite" analogously. Are the sets of soluble and absolutely simple numbers finite or infinite? Do composite non-soluble numbers exist? 3.57 asks for the distribution of non-soluble and simple numbers.
Plan: for a simple group the count is just the number of distinct orders of proper non-trivial subgroups; compute via `ConjugacyClassesSubgroups`/`TableOfMarks` for simple groups up to order ~10⁶ and for non-simple non-soluble groups (SmallGroups ≤ 2000, `PerfectGroup`s, A₅×C_m, S₅×C_m). Then argue: A₅×C_m for suitable m realises every k ≥ some k₀ as non-soluble, so soluble numbers are finite; find explicit composite-non-soluble k (e.g. k not attained by any simple group but attained by A₅×C_m). Score 4 — elementary, finite, definitely yields at least the "composite but not soluble" answer; caveat: low-prestige, obscure problem.

## Score 3

**7.39** (lines 996–1004, J. Mennicke). G = ⟨a,b | a^p=(ab)³=b²=(a^σ b a^{2/σ} b)²=1⟩ maps onto PSL₂(p) with kernel N; N^ab infinite for p=41, σ²≡2; finite for all σ when p=43. (a) Are there infinitely many p with N^ab finite for all σ? (b) Arithmetic condition on σ for N^ab finite?
Plan: for p ≤ ~110 and all σ mod p, build the epimorphism to PSL₂(p) (`GQuotients`), take `Kernel`/`PreImage`, compute `AbelianInvariants` (index ≤ p(p²−1)/2 ≈ 6·10⁵, fine with ACE-backed coset tables). Tabulate which (p, σ) give infinite N^ab; look for a condition on σ (quadratic residuosity, order of σ mod p) — (b) likely solvable as a conjecture backed by data, (a) needs theory. Score 3.

**8.12 a)** (lines 1125–1129, D. L. Johnson, E. F. Robertson). Does the class D0 of finite deficiency-zero groups contain a 3-generator p-group for p ≥ 5? (Also c) bounded derived length of soluble D0-groups; d) which simple groups are composition factors.)
Plan: systematic search of 3-generator/3-relator presentations with short relators (exponents in ±1..±4) whose p-quotient (ANU pq via `EpimorphismPGroup`, `NilpotentQuotient` in nq) stabilises at a finite 5- or 7-group; confirm finiteness with coset enumeration and check d(G)=3 and trivial Schur multiplier (`AbelianInvariantsMultiplier`) as necessary filter. Classic Havas–Newman–Robertson style search, 20 cores make it feasible. Score 3.

**8.23** (lines 1155–1156, L. G. Kovács). If the dihedral group D₁₈ is a section of A×B, must A or B have a section ≅ D₁₈?
Plan: brute force over pairs of small groups: for each pair (A,B) with |A|,|B| ≤ ~150 (restricting to groups having a C₉ or C₂ section but no D₁₈ section), compute whether A×B has a D₁₈ section via `ConjugacyClassesSubgroups` of A×B (for |A×B| ≤ ~2000) and `GQuotients(H, D18)`. Section-closure heuristics reduce the search. A counterexample, if one exists at small order, is found in a day; a proof of "yes" would need theory (known for D_{2p}, p prime). Score 3.

**8.3** (lines 1079–1091, B. A. F. Wehrfritz). For which m, n is the p-group P_n(Z/p^m) (unitriangular mod p on the diagonal, entries below diagonal ≡ 0 mod p) regular? Known: regular if mn<p, if n²<p, and cases m=1, m=2 done.
Plan: first open cases p=5: (n,m)=(3,3),(3,4),(4,3); p=7: (3,4),(4,3),(3,5). Build the group in GAP as matrices over `ZmodnZ(p^m)`, convert with `IsomorphismPcGroup`, then test regularity ((xy)^p ≡ x^p y^p mod ℧₁(⟨x,y⟩')) on random pairs and on all pairs of generators; an irregular pair is a proof of irregularity. Aim: conjecture the exact boundary in (n,m,p) and prove the irregular side. Score 3.

**8.85** (lines 1325–1327, E. I. Khukhro). Construct a finite p-group whose Hughes subgroup H_p(G) = ⟨x : |x| ≠ p⟩ is non-trivial of index p³. (Wall's examples give index p² for p=5,7.)
Plan: search for quotients of the free 3-generator group of exponent-p class c (ANU pq / LiePRing package) in which the elements of order p generate a subgroup of index exactly p³; use Wall's Lie-ring criterion (elements outside index-p³ subgroup have order p ⇔ identities in the associated Lie ring) and search over class ≤ ~12 for p = 5, 7. Heavy but well-defined p-quotient computation. Score 3.

**5.54** (lines 696–699, J. Wiegold). For distinct primes p,q,r and commutator word u(x,y,z), show A_n is generated by ξ,η,ζ with ξ^p=η^q=ζ^r=ξηζ·u(ξ,η,ζ)=1 for (infinitely many) n.
Plan: for fixed (p,q,r,u), e.g. (2,3,5,[x,y]) or (2,3,7,[[x,y],z]), form the fp group Γ and run `GQuotients(Γ, AlternatingGroup(n))` or `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup(Γ, n)` for n ≤ 15–20; this settles existence for specific n. "Infinitely many n" would need Conder-style coset-diagram gluing — a longer project. Score 3 (for the concrete existence part).

**6.47** (lines 842–845, E. I. Khukhro / C. D. H. Cooper). If a word v(x,y) defines a new group operation x⊙y=v(x,y) on the set G, does G_v lie in the variety generated by G?
Plan: for small finite G (orders ≤ 64) and all words v of length ≤ 6–8, test group axioms on G directly; for each genuine G_v, test membership in var(G) by checking whether G_v is a quotient of the relatively free group of var(G) of rank d(G_v) (a subgroup of G^{|G|^d}, computable for tiny G) or by checking all laws of G up to a length bound. Look for G_v with an element whose ⊙-order exceeds exp(G) or failing a law of G. Score 3 — a counterexample, if one exists, is likely small.

**7.27** (lines 945–950, V. M. Levchuk). For large q, does SL_n(q) contain a diagonal matrix lying in no proper irreducible subgroup other than block-monomial ones? Known for n=2,3.
Plan: n=4 (then 5) for q ranging over 5..31: use `ClassicalMaximals` package to list maximal subgroups of SL₄(q); for a candidate diagonal element (distinct eigenvalues generating F_q^*, chosen to avoid field-extension subgroups) test membership in each conjugacy class of irreducible maximals via `IsConjugate`/fixed-point arguments. Data suggests the general Aschbacher-class argument. Score 3.

**7.31** (lines 965–969, V. D. Mazurov). If A ≤ Aut(G) acts transitively on the involutions of a finite non-abelian 2-group G, must A be soluble?
Plan: for all 2-groups of order ≤ 2⁸ (and filtered subsets of 2⁹, e.g. those with all involutions of the same "type"), compute `AutomorphismGroup`, check transitivity on involutions, then `IsSolvable`. Gross's classification narrows candidates to few classes (Suzuki 2-groups, etc.); target the class not covered by Bryukhanova. Score 3 (counterexample unlikely at small order, but a clean verified bound is progress).

**4.24 a)** (lines 463–470, D. M. Goldschmidt). T a non-abelian Sylow 2-subgroup of a finite simple group, of class n: what is the best bound for exp(T)? (Trivial bound 2^{n(n−1)}.)
Plan: tabulate (class, exponent) of Sylow 2-subgroups for all simple groups in the ATLAS/Small orders and for the families (dihedral/semidihedral/wreath types in PSL₂, PSL₃, PSU₃, A_n, Suzuki) — data strongly suggests exp(T) ≤ 2^n with dihedral attaining it. Then a CFSG case check by families gives the answer. Score 3.

**9.45** (lines 1474–1478, Yu. D. Popov, I. V. Protasov). For rational a ∈ R^n, S(a) = Zа + Z^n; find necessary and sufficient conditions on the coordinates of a for S(a) to have an orthogonal basis.
Plan: S(a) = (1/q)·(lattice generated by qZ^n and the integer vector qa); a lattice has an orthogonal basis iff its Gram matrix is Z-equivalent to a diagonal form — test via enumerating short vectors (`ShortestVectors`, `LLLReducedGramMat`) for n=2,3 over all a with small denominators; conjecture and prove a condition (for n=2 almost certainly provable in a day: relates to representing the norm form as sum of two squares). Score 3.

## Score 2

**4.13** (lines 445–446, Berkovich). Every finite non-abelian p-group has a non-inner automorphism of order p. Plan: verify for all groups of order 2⁸, 3⁷, 5⁶, 7⁵ via `AutomorphismGroup` (many classes already proved; check literature to avoid duplication). Verification only; no counterexample expected. Score 2.

**6.21** (lines 765–771, Mazurov). Best Higman function χ(p) for fixed-point-free automorphisms of order p; conjecture χ(p)=(p²−1)/4; known p ≤ 7. Plan: first open case p=11 via Lie rings graded by Z/11 with L₀=0 (Kreknin–Higman reduction); a computer search for the class of the free "Z/11-graded, L₀=0" Lie ring is enormous, but restricted computations (Lie algebras of small dimension over GF(2), GF(3), search for class 30 examples vs. proof of ≤30) may be feasible with LieAlgDB/LiePRing. Score 2.

**8.77** (lines 1285–1288, Fon-Der-Flaass). Do srg(v,k,0,2) exist with k>10? Feasibility forces k−1 a square; the first feasible open parameter set is (352,26,0,2). Plan: search assuming a prescribed automorphism group (e.g. an involution-rich group acting with few orbits) using GAP + SAT/orbit-matrix methods; exhaustive search is out of reach. Score 2.

**5.55** (lines 701–703, Wiegold). Find a finite p-group not embeddable in a finite p-group with trivial Schur multiplier. Plan: computational hunt for obstructions is unclear (embedding target unbounded); likely needs a theoretical invariant. Score 2.

**5.56 a)** (lines 705–707, Wiegold). For p>3, does every finite exponent-p group embed in the derived subgroup of a finite exponent-p group? Plan: check small exponent-5 groups (orders 5³, 5⁴) against the derived subgroup of R(2,5) (order 5³⁴) and of R(3,5)-class quotients via pq; positive small evidence only. Score 2.

**7.57 a)** (lines 1041–1046, Churkin). Is there a finitely presented G with r_M(G) = d(G)+r(G) for some basis M? Plan: small finite groups where relation counts are known exactly (via multiplier lower bounds) and search over generating sets; hard because r_M is not computable in general. Score 2.

**5.26 a)** (lines 613–624, H. Koch). Find a finite p-group with r₁ > r₂ (discrete vs. pro-p relation count). Plan: relation-gap type question; candidate groups with d(M(G)) small but efficiency failing; lower bounds for r₁ are the obstacle. Score 2.

**7.15** (lines 901–904, Griess). If F*(G) quasisimple and α an involutory automorphism, C_G(α) contains an involution outside Z(F*(G)) unless quaternion Sylow 2. Plan: verify for all quasisimple groups in AtlasRep with their automorphism groups; a full proof is CFSG family-by-family and probably exists in GLS. Score 2.

**9.28** (lines 1406–1410, Makhnëv). Finite G generated by a class D of involutions such that D₁,…,D_n (products of i distinct commuting elements of D) exhaust the involution classes; Fi22, Fi23 satisfy this with n=3. Plan: run through all ATLAS groups and 3-transposition groups computing D_i sets; yields a list, not a classification. Score 2.

**8.82** (lines 1299–1312, Helling). Compute r(π) = dim H₁(Γ₀(π)\H³, Q) for Bianchi groups over Q(√D), D<0. Plan: these are Bianchi-modular-form ranks; Cremona/Şengün/Page tables and software (Magma, Bianchi.gp) already compute them for many π; a table can be produced but no closed form is expected. Score 2.

**8.4** (lines 1094–1095, Vaughan-Lee). Finite nilpotent loop with no finite basis of laws. Plan: loop package (LOOPS) enumeration of small nilpotent loops and testing candidate infinite law families; needs a theoretical non-finite-basis argument. Score 2.

## Noted but not ranked
- **8.35 c)** (lines 1182–1184): maximal subgroups of the Monster — although not starred in this edition, this was completed by Dietrich–Lee–Popiel (2023, arXiv:2304.14646). Not a day-scale computation; effectively already solved.
- **9.24** (lines 1399–1401) Thompson's G = CC conjecture and **4.65** (lines 551–556) Feit–Thompson divisibility conjecture: well known, extensively computer-checked already; no realistic day-scale resolution. Score 1.

## Top 5
1. **8.44** — compute G_p for p = 29, 37, 41, …: finiteness (ACE) or infiniteness (low-index subgroups / hyperbolicity); each new p is a definite result and the general claim is attackable by one-relator-quotient methods.
2. **2.78/3.57** — purely elementary counting of subgroup orders in simple and non-soluble groups; GAP data plus an A₅×C_m construction very likely settles all three questions of 2.78.
3. **7.39** — exhaustive (p, σ) table of N^ab for p ≤ 110 is a straightforward GAP computation and will almost certainly reveal the arithmetic condition asked in (b).
4. **8.3** — first open cases (p=5, n=3, m=3, …) are decidable by explicit regularity tests on pc-groups; irregular pairs give proofs.
5. **8.12 a)** — a classic presentation search (pq/nq + coset enumeration) for a 3-generator deficiency-zero 5-group; well-trodden method, real chance of a new example with 20 cores.</result>

## Score 4

**8.44** (lines 1206–1211, J. Mennicke). Groups G_p = ⟨a,b | a²=b^p=(ab)³=(b^r a b^{−2r} a)²=1⟩ with r²+1≡0 (mod p). Prove/disprove that G_p is infinite for all but finitely many p; known finite for p ≤ 17 (by computer).
Plan: first open cases p = 29, 37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97. In GAP: coset enumeration (ACE package, large tables) for finiteness; for infiniteness use `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup` + `AbelianInvariants` (a finite-index subgroup with infinite abelianisation), or KBMAG/`IsHyperbolic` (kbmag/walrus) since G_p is a one-relator quotient of the hyperbolic (2,3,p) triangle group; curvature/small-cancellation arguments (Edjvet–Howie style) could then give the "all but finitely many" statement. Score 4 — a direct computation settles each new p; the general statement is plausible with known one-relator-quotient techniques.

**2.78 + 3.57** (lines 292–303 and 411–412, P. I. Trofimov). An "IEn̄-system" of a finite G is the set of all subgroups of a given order containing a non-normal one; k is "soluble" if every group with exactly k systems is soluble, "simple/absolutely simple/composite" analogously. Are the sets of soluble and absolutely simple numbers finite or infinite? Do composite non-soluble numbers exist? 3.57 asks for the distribution of non-soluble and simple numbers.
Plan: for a simple group the count is just the number of distinct orders of proper non-trivial subgroups; compute via `ConjugacyClassesSubgroups`/`TableOfMarks` for simple groups up to order ~10⁶ and for non-simple non-soluble groups (SmallGroups ≤ 2000, `PerfectGroup`s, A₅×C_m, S₅×C_m). Then argue: A₅×C_m for suitable m realises every k ≥ some k₀ as non-soluble, so soluble numbers are finite; find explicit composite-non-soluble k (e.g. k not attained by any simple group but attained by A₅×C_m). Score 4 — elementary, finite, definitely yields at least the "composite but not soluble" answer; caveat: low-prestige, obscure problem.

## Score 3

**7.39** (lines 996–1004, J. Mennicke). G = ⟨a,b | a^p=(ab)³=b²=(a^σ b a^{2/σ} b)²=1⟩ maps onto PSL₂(p) with kernel N; N^ab infinite for p=41, σ²≡2; finite for all σ when p=43. (a) Are there infinitely many p with N^ab finite for all σ? (b) Arithmetic condition on σ for N^ab finite?
Plan: for p ≤ ~110 and all σ mod p, build the epimorphism to PSL₂(p) (`GQuotients`), take `Kernel`/`PreImage`, compute `AbelianInvariants` (index ≤ p(p²−1)/2 ≈ 6·10⁵, fine with ACE-backed coset tables). Tabulate which (p, σ) give infinite N^ab; look for a condition on σ (quadratic residuosity, order of σ mod p) — (b) likely solvable as a conjecture backed by data, (a) needs theory. Score 3.

**8.12 a)** (lines 1125–1129, D. L. Johnson, E. F. Robertson). Does the class D0 of finite deficiency-zero groups contain a 3-generator p-group for p ≥ 5? (Also c) bounded derived length of soluble D0-groups; d) which simple groups are composition factors.)
Plan: systematic search of 3-generator/3-relator presentations with short relators (exponents in ±1..±4) whose p-quotient (ANU pq via `EpimorphismPGroup`, `NilpotentQuotient` in nq) stabilises at a finite 5- or 7-group; confirm finiteness with coset enumeration and check d(G)=3 and trivial Schur multiplier (`AbelianInvariantsMultiplier`) as necessary filter. Classic Havas–Newman–Robertson style search, 20 cores make it feasible. Score 3.

**8.23** (lines 1155–1156, L. G. Kovács). If the dihedral group D₁₈ is a section of A×B, must A or B have a section ≅ D₁₈?
Plan: brute force over pairs of small groups: for each pair (A,B) with |A|,|B| ≤ ~150 (restricting to groups having a C₉ or C₂ section but no D₁₈ section), compute whether A×B has a D₁₈ section via `ConjugacyClassesSubgroups` of A×B (for |A×B| ≤ ~2000) and `GQuotients(H, D18)`. Section-closure heuristics reduce the search. A counterexample, if one exists at small order, is found in a day; a proof of "yes" would need theory (known for D_{2p}, p prime). Score 3.

**8.3** (lines 1079–1091, B. A. F. Wehrfritz). For which m, n is the p-group P_n(Z/p^m) (unitriangular mod p on the diagonal, entries below diagonal ≡ 0 mod p) regular? Known: regular if mn<p, if n²<p, and cases m=1, m=2 done.
Plan: first open cases p=5: (n,m)=(3,3),(3,4),(4,3); p=7: (3,4),(4,3),(3,5). Build the group in GAP as matrices over `ZmodnZ(p^m)`, convert with `IsomorphismPcGroup`, then test regularity ((xy)^p ≡ x^p y^p mod ℧₁(⟨x,y⟩')) on random pairs and on all pairs of generators; an irregular pair is a proof of irregularity. Aim: conjecture the exact boundary in (n,m,p) and prove the irregular side. Score 3.

**8.85** (lines 1325–1327, E. I. Khukhro). Construct a finite p-group whose Hughes subgroup H_p(G) = ⟨x : |x| ≠ p⟩ is non-trivial of index p³. (Wall's examples give index p² for p=5,7.)
Plan: search for quotients of the free 3-generator group of exponent-p class c (ANU pq / LiePRing package) in which the elements of order p generate a subgroup of index exactly p³; use Wall's Lie-ring criterion (elements outside index-p³ subgroup have order p ⇔ identities in the associated Lie ring) and search over class ≤ ~12 for p = 5, 7. Heavy but well-defined p-quotient computation. Score 3.

**5.54** (lines 696–699, J. Wiegold). For distinct primes p,q,r and commutator word u(x,y,z), show A_n is generated by ξ,η,ζ with ξ^p=η^q=ζ^r=ξηζ·u(ξ,η,ζ)=1 for (infinitely many) n.
Plan: for fixed (p,q,r,u), e.g. (2,3,5,[x,y]) or (2,3,7,[[x,y],z]), form the fp group Γ and run `GQuotients(Γ, AlternatingGroup(n))` or `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup(Γ, n)` for n ≤ 15–20; this settles existence for specific n. "Infinitely many n" would need Conder-style coset-diagram gluing — a longer project. Score 3 (for the concrete existence part).

Plan: for small finite G (orders ≤ 64) and all words v of length ≤ 6–8, test group axioms on G directly; for each genuine G_v, test membership in var(G) by checking whether G_v is a quotient of the relatively free group of var(G) of rank d(G_v) (a subgroup of G^{|G|^d}, computable for tiny G) or by checking all laws of G up to a length bound. Look for G_v with an element whose ⊙-order exceeds exp(G) or failing a law of G. Score 3 — a counterexample, if one exists, is likely small.

Plan: n=4 (then 5) for q ranging over 5..31: use `ClassicalMaximals` package to list maximal subgroups of SL₄(q); for a candidate diagonal element (distinct eigenvalues generating F_q^*, chosen to avoid field-extension subgroups) test membership in each conjugacy class of irreducible maximals via `IsConjugate`/fixed-point arguments. Data suggests the general Aschbacher-class argument. Score 3.

Plan: for all 2-groups of order ≤ 2⁸ (and filtered subsets of 2⁹, e.g. those with all involutions of the same "type"), compute `AutomorphismGroup`, check transitivity on involutions, then `IsSolvable`. Gross's classification narrows candidates to few classes (Suzuki 2-groups, etc.); target the class not covered by Bryukhanova. Score 3 (counterexample unlikely at small order, but a clean verified bound is progress).

**4.24 a)** (lines 463–470, D. M. Goldschmidt). T a non-abelian Sylow 2-subgroup of a finite simple group, of class n: what is the best bound for exp(T)? (Trivial bound 2^{n(n−1)}.)
Plan: tabulate (class, exponent) of Sylow 2-subgroups for all simple groups in the ATLAS/Small orders and for the families (dihedral/semidihedral/wreath types in PSL₂, PSL₃, PSU₃, A_n, Suzuki) — data strongly suggests exp(T) ≤ 2^n with dihedral attaining it. Then a CFSG case check by families gives the answer. Score 3.

**9.45** (lines 1474–1478, Yu. D. Popov, I. V. Protasov). For rational a ∈ R^n, S(a) = Zа + Z^n; find necessary and sufficient conditions on the coordinates of a for S(a) to have an orthogonal basis.

Score 3.

Finite G generated by a class D of involutions such that D₁,…,D_n (products of i distinct commuting elements of D) exhaust the involution classes; Fi22, Fi23 satisfy this with n=3. Plan: run through all ATLAS groups and 3-transposition groups computing D_i sets; yields a list, not a classification. Score 2.

Build the group in GAP as matrices over `ZmodnZ(p^m)`, convert with `IsomorphismPcGroup`, then test regularity ((xy)^p ≡ x^p y^p mod ℧₁(⟨x,y⟩')) on random pairs and on all pairs of generators; an irregular pair is a proof of irregularity. Aim: conjecture the exact boundary in (n,m,p) and prove the irregular side. Score 3.

**8.85** (lines 1325–1327, E. I. Khukhro). Construct a finite p-group whose Hughes subgroup H_p(G) = ⟨x : |x| ≠ p⟩ is non-trivial of index p³. (Wall's examples give index p² for p=5,7.)
Plan: search for quotients of the free 3-generator group of exponent-p class c (ANU pq / LiePRing package) in which the elements of order p generate a subgroup of index exactly p³; use Wall's Lie-ring criterion (elements outside index-p³ subgroup have order p ⇔ identities in the associated Lie ring) and search over class ≤ ~12 for p = 5, 7. Heavy but well-defined p-quotient computation. Score 3.

**5.54** (lines 696–699, J. Wiegold). For distinct primes p,q,r and commutator word u(x,y,z), show A_n is generated by ξ,η,ζ with ξ^p=η^q=ζ^r=ξηζ·u(ξ,η,ζ)=1 for (infinitely many) n.
Plan: for fixed (p,q,r,u), e.g. (2,3,5,[x,y]) or (2,3,7,[[x,y],z]), form the fp group Γ and run `GQuotients(Γ, AlternatingGroup(n))` or `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup(Γ, n)` for n ≤ 15–20; this settles existence for specific n. "Infinitely many n" would need Conder-style coset-diagram gluing — a longer project. Score 3 (for the concrete existence part).

**6.47** (lines 842–845, E. I. Khukhro / C. D. H. Cooper). If a word v(x,y) defines a new group operation x⊙y=v(x,y) on the set G, does G_v lie in the variety generated by G?
Plan: for small finite G (orders ≤ 64) and all words v of length ≤ 6–8, test group axioms on G directly; for each genuine G_v, test membership in var(G) by checking whether G_v is a quotient of the relatively free group of var(G) of rank d(G_v) (a subgroup of G^{|G|^d}, computable for tiny G) or by checking all laws of G up to a length bound. Look for G_v with an element whose ⊙-order exceeds exp(G) or failing a law of G. Score 3 — a counterexample, if one exists, is likely small.

**7.27** (lines 945–950, V. M. Levchuk). For large q, does SL_n(q) contain a diagonal matrix lying in no proper irreducible subgroup other than block-monomial ones? Known for n=2,3.
Plan: n=4 (then 5) for q ranging over 5..31: use `ClassicalMaximals` package to list maximal subgroups of SL₄(q); for a candidate diagonal element (distinct eigenvalues generating F_q^*, chosen to avoid field-extension subgroups) test membership in each conjugacy class of irreducible maximals via `IsConjugate`/fixed-point arguments. Data suggests the general Aschbacher-class argument. Score 3.

**7.31** (lines 965–969, V. D. Mazurov). If A ≤ Aut(G) acts transitively on the involutions of a finite non-abelian 2-group G, must A be soluble?
Plan: for all 2-groups of order ≤ 2⁸ (and filtered subsets of 2⁹, e.g. those with all involutions of the same "type"), compute `AutomorphismGroup`, check transitivity on involutions, then `IsSolvable`. Gross's classification narrows candidates to few classes (Suzuki 2-groups, etc.); target the class not covered by Bryukhanova. Score 3 (counterexample unlikely at small order, but a clean verified bound is progress).

**4.24 a)** (lines 463–470, D. M. Goldschmidt). T a non-abelian Sylow 2-subgroup of a finite simple group, of class n: what is the best bound for exp(T)? (Trivial bound 2^{n(n−1)}.)
Plan: tabulate (class, exponent) of Sylow 2-subgroups for all simple groups in the ATLAS/Small orders and for the families (dihedral/semidihedral/wreath types in PSL₂, PSL₃, PSU₃, A_n, Suzuki) — data strongly suggests exp(T) ≤ 2^n with dihedral attaining it. Then a CFSG case check by families gives the answer. Score 3.

**9.45** (lines 1474–1478, Yu. D. Popov, I. V. Protasov). For rational a ∈ R^n, S(a) = Zа + Z^n; find necessary and sufficient conditions on the coordinates of a for S(a) to have an orthogonal basis.
Plan: S(a) = (1/q)·(lattice generated by qZ^n and the integer vector qa); a lattice has an orthogonal basis iff its Gram matrix is Z-equivalent to a diagonal form — test via enumerating short vectors (`ShortestVectors`, `LLLReducedGramMat`) for n=2,3 over all a with small denominators; conjecture and prove a condition (for n=2 almost certainly provable in a day: relates to representing the norm form as sum of two squares). Score 3.

## Score 2

**4.13** (lines 445–446, Berkovich). Every finite non-abelian p-group has a non-inner automorphism of order p. Plan: verify for all groups of order 2⁸, 3⁷, 5⁶, 7⁵ via `AutomorphismGroup` (many classes already proved; check literature to avoid duplication). Verification only; no counterexample expected. Score 2.

**6.21** (lines 765–771, Mazurov). Best Higman function χ(p) for fixed-point-free automorphisms of order p; conjecture χ(p)=(p²−1)/4; known p ≤ 7. Plan: first open case p=11 via Lie rings graded by Z/11 with L₀=0 (Kreknin–Higman reduction); a computer search for the class of the free "Z/11-graded, L₀=0" Lie ring is enormous, but restricted computations (Lie algebras of small dimension over GF(2), GF(3), search for class 30 examples vs. proof of ≤30) may be feasible with LieAlgDB/LiePRing. Score 2.

**8.77** (lines 1285–1288, Fon-Der-Flaass). Do srg(v,k,0,2) exist with k>10? Feasibility forces k−1 a square; the first feasible open parameter set is (352,26,0,2). Plan: search assuming a prescribed automorphism group (e.g. an involution-rich group acting with few orbits) using GAP + SAT/orbit-matrix methods; exhaustive search is out of reach. Score 2.

**5.55** (lines 701–703, Wiegold). Find a finite p-group not embeddable in a finite p-group with trivial Schur multiplier. Plan: computational hunt for obstructions is unclear (embedding target unbounded); likely needs a theoretical invariant. Score 2.

**5.56 a)** (lines 705–707, Wiegold). For p>3, does every finite exponent-p group embed in the derived subgroup of a finite exponent-p group? Plan: check small exponent-5 groups (orders 5³, 5⁴) against the derived subgroup of R(2,5) (order 5³⁴) and of R(3,5)-class quotients via pq; positive small evidence only. Score 2.

**7.57 a)** (lines 1041–1046, Churkin). Is there a finitely presented G with r_M(G) = d(G)+r(G) for some basis M? Plan: small finite groups where relation counts are known exactly (via multiplier lower bounds) and search over generating sets; hard because r_M is not computable in general. Score 2.

**5.26 a)** (lines 613–624, H. Koch). Find a finite p-group with r₁ > r₂ (discrete vs. pro-p relation count). Plan: relation-gap type question; candidate groups with d(M(G)) small but efficiency failing; lower bounds for r₁ are the obstacle. Score 2.

**7.15** (lines 901–904, Griess). If F*(G) quasisimple and α an involutory automorphism, C_G(α) contains an involution outside Z(F*(G)) unless quaternion Sylow 2. Plan: verify for all quasisimple groups in AtlasRep with their automorphism groups; a full proof is CFSG family-by-family and probably exists in GLS. Score 2.

**9.28** (lines 1406–1410, Makhnëv). Finite G generated by a class D of involutions such that D₁,…,D_n (products of i distinct commuting elements of D) exhaust the involution classes; Fi22, Fi23 satisfy this with n=3. Plan: run through all ATLAS groups and 3-transposition groups computing D_i sets; yields a list, not a classification. Score 2.

**8.82** (lines 1299–1312, Helling). Compute r(π) = dim H₁(Γ₀(π)\H³, Q) for Bianchi groups over Q(√D), D<0. Plan: these are Bianchi-modular-form ranks; Cremona/Şengün/Page tables and software (Magma, Bianchi.gp) already compute them for many π; a table can be produced but no closed form is expected. Score 2.

**8.4** (lines 1094–1095, Vaughan-Lee). Finite nilpotent loop with no finite basis of laws. Plan: loop package (LOOPS) enumeration of small nilpotent loops and testing candidate infinite law families; needs a theoretical non-finite-basis argument. Score 2.

## Noted but not ranked
- **8.35 c)** (lines 1182–1184): maximal subgroups of the Monster — although not starred in this edition, this was completed by Dietrich–Lee–Popiel (2023, arXiv:2304.14646). Not a day-scale computation; effectively already solved.
- **9.24** (lines 1399–1401) Thompson's G = CC conjecture and **4.65** (lines 551–556) Feit–Thompson divisibility conjecture: well known, extensively computer-checked already; no realistic day-scale resolution. Score 1.

## Top 5
1. **8.44** — compute G_p for p = 29, 37, 41, …: finiteness (ACE) or infiniteness (low-index subgroups / hyperbolicity); each new p is a definite result and the general claim is attackable by one-relator-quotient methods.
2. **2.78/3.57** — purely elementary counting of subgroup orders in simple and non-soluble groups; GAP data plus an A₅×C_m construction very likely settles all three questions of 2.78.
3. **7.39** — exhaustive (p, σ) table of N^ab for p ≤ 110 is a straightforward GAP computation and will almost certainly reveal the arithmetic condition asked in (b).
4. **8.3** — first open cases (p=5, n=3, m=3, …) are decidable by explicit regularity tests on pc-groups; irregular pairs give proofs.
5. **8.12 a)** — a classic presentation search (pq/nq + coset enumeration) for a 3-generator deficiency-zero 5-group; well-trodden method, real chance of a new example with 20 cores.</result>

<result>## Kourovka Notebook, issues 14–16 (file lines 3163–4883): tractable-problem triage

Read completely. Problems already marked answered (∗ with "Yes/No/…" comment) were skipped: 14.4, 14.5(b,d), 14.19, 14.20, 14.23, 14.54, 14.69(a), 14.85, 14.98, 14.102, 15.14(b), 15.19(b), 15.26, 15.40, 15.45(a), 15.53, 15.70, 15.80, 16.11, 16.48, 16.51. Everything below is still open in the 21st edition.

### Candidates, ranked by tractability score

**1. 16.60 (MacHale) — score 4.** Lines 4675–4681. T(G) = sum of irreducible character degrees; for α ∈ Aut G let S_α = {g : α(g) = g⁻¹}. Is T(G) ≥ |S_α| always? (For α = id this is the classical Frobenius–Schur bound T(G) ≥ #involutions+1; the Aut-version is open.)
Attack: GAP loop over all SmallGroups of order ≤ 511 (and selected larger orders): `AutomorphismGroup`, for each automorphism (reps up to conjugacy in Aut G suffice) count inverted elements, compare with `Sum(CharacterDegrees)`. Pure finite search; a counterexample settles it, and the search is cheap enough to cover every order ≤ 1000 except 512/768.

**2. 15.2(a)+(b) (Isaacs) — score 4.** Lines 3789–3801. x is nonvanishing if χ(x) ≠ 0 for all χ ∈ Irr(G). (a) In a solvable G, must a nonvanishing element of even order lie in F(G)? (odd order: yes, Isaacs–Navarro–Wolf.) (b) Which nonabelian simple groups have nontrivial nonvanishing elements (A7 does)?
Attack: (a) loop over solvable groups of order ≤ 2000 (skip prime-power orders, 512, 1024, 1536), `CharacterTable`, find columns with no zero, test `in FittingSubgroup`. (b) is a direct scan of every table in CTblLib (all sporadic, ATLAS Lie-type, A_n up to large n via `CharacterTable("Symmetric"/"Alternating")`): a complete answer for all groups with library tables is a well-defined special case; A_n can then be attacked with Murnaghan–Nakayama vanishing criteria.

**3. 14.44 (Kazarin–Sangroniz) — score 4.** Lines 3440–3444. G = AB with gcd(|A|,|B|) = 1: is k(G) ≤ k(A)k(B)? (Fails without coprimeness; true if A or B normal.)
Attack: for every non-prime-power order ≤ 2000 (minus 512/1024/1536), take conjugacy classes of subgroups, pick pairs with coprime orders multiplying to |G| (then G = AB automatically), compare `NrConjugacyClasses`. Add the coprime factorisations of simple groups (Arad–Fisman / Liebeck–Praeger–Saxl list: A_p = A_{p−1}·C_p, L2(q) cases, etc.) via character tables. Counterexample or exhaustive small-order verification in a day.

**4. 16.14 (Berkovich) — score 4.** Lines 4491–4492. Finite 2-group with Ω1(G) ≤ Z(G): is rank(G/G²) ≤ 2·rank Z(G)?
Attack: loop over all 2-groups of order ≤ 2^8 (56 092) and 2^9 (10.5 M, feasible on 20 cores with the cheap tests `Omega`, `Centre`, `RankPGroup(G/Frattini)`). A counterexample settles it; a "yes" at these orders is at least strong evidence and might suggest a proof.

**5. 15.74 (Pálfy) — score 4 for the first open case p = 5.** Lines 4240–4242. For each prime p find a p-group of class p whose normal-subgroup lattice does not embed in the subgroup lattice of any abelian group (done for p = 2, 3; class < p is impossible by the Lazard/Baer correspondence).
Attack: enumerate 5-groups of class 5 of order 5^6, 5^7 (SmallGroups), compute `NormalSubgroups` lattice, test the Arguesian identity (subgroup lattices of abelian groups are Arguesian; also Haiman's higher Arguesian identities). Modular-lattice pruning keeps the 6-tuple search small. One non-Arguesian example settles p = 5.

**6. 14.74 (Pyber) — score 3.** Lines 3613–3615. Is k(G) ≤ ∏ k(P_i) over Sylow subgroups of G?
Attack: same loop as item 3 (trivial for p-groups): `NrConjugacyClasses(G)` vs product over `SylowSubgroup`. Then simple/almost-simple groups from CTblLib with Sylow subgroups computed in permutation representations. Cheap; counterexample unlikely at small orders but the search is complete and fast.

**7. 15.29 (Mann) / 16.63 (MacHale) — score 3.** Lines 3927–3929 / 4684–4685. Is D8 the only nontrivial p-group with G ≅ Aut G? Is there a p-group of odd order with |Aut G| = |G|?
Attack: `AutPGrp` over all groups of order 3^7, 3^8 (1.4 M), 5^6, 5^7, 7^6, 2^8, 2^9; filter |Aut G| = |G| (equivalently |Out G| = |Z(G)|, Aut G a p-group). Note the divisibility conjecture |G| | |Aut G| fails in general (González-Sánchez–Jaikin-Zapirain), so examples may exist but probably above library range; hits would be decisive.

**8. 15.30 (Berkovich) — score 3.** Lines 3933–3934. Is every finite abelian p-group the Schur multiplier of some nonabelian p-group?
Attack: tabulate `AbelianInvariantsMultiplier` for all groups of order p^n (p = 2,3,5; n ≤ 7) to see what occurs; then build a construction from metacyclic p-groups (cyclic multiplier of prescribed order, explicit formulas) and the Künneth formula M(G×H) = M(G)×M(H)×(G^ab⊗H^ab). Likely a short constructive answer.

**9. 15.3 (Isaacs) — score 3.** Lines 3803–3810. Does a solvable group have faithful nonlinear irreducible α, β with αβ irreducible? (Nonsolvable examples: SL2(5), A_{n²}; Isaacs 2000 gives evidence for "no".)
Attack: loop over solvable SmallGroups (orders ≤ 2000 minus big 2-power orders), compute tables, test all pairs of faithful nonlinear irreducibles with α(1)β(1) dividing |G| via `ScalarProduct`. Full search in a day; a "no" proof needs theory.

**10. 15.99 (Shi) — score 3.** Lines 4404–4407. Does f(n) = k (number of groups of order n) have a solution for every k? Verified for k ≤ 1000.
Attack: extend the verified range with `NumberSmallGroups`, the Cubefree package, and closed formulas for orders p^a q, squarefree, etc.; search n with few prime factors so f(n) is small and controllable. A day gives k ≤ 10^4–10^5, not a proof.

**11. 16.26 (Vasil'ev) — score 3.** Lines 4537–4542. Is there k such that no k pairwise non-isomorphic simple groups share the same prime (Gruenberg–Kegel) graph? Conjecture k = 5 (i.e., at most 4 share).
Attack: compute GK-graphs of all simple groups up to a large order bound using Buturlakin's spectrum formulas / CTblLib tables, and search for 5 groups with a common graph (refutes the conjectured k = 5). Proving a bound needs theory.

**12. 15.83 (Merzlyakov/Sosnovskii) — score 3.** Lines 4292–4295. Is there rational α, |α| < 2, with ⟨(1 α;0 1),(1 0;α 1)⟩ free? Conjugating gives the (1,λ) normalization with λ = α²; Kim–Koberda (Michigan Math. J. 2022) proved non-freeness for λ = s/r with s ≤ 27 (s ≠ 24), i.e., α = p/q with p ≤ 5 is done; open for p ≥ 6 (α = 6/5, 7/4, 7/5, 7/6, 9/5, 11/6, …).
Attack: computer search for relations for specific new α (exact rational arithmetic word enumeration, Chorna–Geller–Shpilrain / Kim–Koberda techniques). Settles individual α; not the general question.

**13. 15.84 (Sosnovskii) — score 3.** Lines 4300–4306. Rational α, β, γ each with |·| < 3 such that (1 α;0 1), (1 0;β 1), (1−γ −γ; γ 1+γ) generate a free group of rank 3? (Three parabolics fixing ∞, 0, −1.)
Attack: computer-assisted ping-pong: search rational parameters near 3 with disjoint fundamental domains in the upper half-plane, verified by interval arithmetic. A positive answer is plausibly obtainable in a day.

**14. 15.95 (Mann–Praeger) — score 3.** Lines 4373–4377. Transitive p-group all of whose fixed-point-free elements have order p: must it have exponent p? True for p = 2, 3.
Attack: first open case p = 5: search groups of order 5^6, 5^7 with each core-free subgroup H (action on cosets), check derangements' orders vs exponent; also transitive groups of degree 25 from TransitiveGroups. A counterexample settles "no".

**15. 16.33 (Glauberman) — score 3.** Lines 4569–4580. p-group with abelian A of order p^n: does it contain abelian B of order p^n normal in ⟨B^G⟩, for p = 3 (a) and p = 2 (b); elementary abelian version for p = 3 (c)? (True for larger p; D32 kills (c) for p = 2.)
Attack: all 3-groups of order ≤ 3^8 and 2-groups ≤ 2^9: compute maximal abelian subgroup order, then test each abelian B of that order for B ⊴ `NormalClosure(G,B)`. A counterexample is possible in this range.

**16. 14.67 (Mukhamet'yanov–Fomin) — score 3.** Lines 3553–3556. a ≠ 1 with |C_G(a)| maximal among nontrivial elements; H nilpotent normalized by C_G(a): is H ≤ C_G(a)? (True if H abelian or H a p'-group for p ∈ π(Z(C_G(a))).)
Attack: loop over groups of order ≤ 1000: find such a, then for every conjugacy class of nilpotent subgroups H test whether `Normalizer(G,H)` contains a conjugate of C_G(a) and H ⊄ that conjugate. Complete finite search.

**17. 16.46 (Conder) — score 3.** Lines 4632–4643. Explicit 6-generator, 20-relator presentation K (index-8 subgroup of an amalgam of arc-transitive groups on the 3-valent tree): does K have a nontrivial finite quotient?
Attack: `LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup` up to index 40+, `GQuotients` onto all simple groups of order ≤ 10^7, p-quotient/soluble-quotient algorithms, and quotients modulo the normal closure of subwords. Any hit answers "yes"; "no" would be a striking finitely presented group with no finite quotients and is out of reach.

**18. 16.45 (Cameron) — score 3.** Lines 4618–4630. b(G) = max minimal-base size over all permutation representations; μ′(G) = max size of an independent set. Is b(G) = μ′(G)? (b ≤ μ′ known; equality for S_n.) Equivalent: maximal Boolean lattice B(n) meet-embedded in the subgroup lattice can be chosen with normal bottom.
Attack: for small groups compute μ′(G) (independent subsets via subgroup lattice) and the lattice-embedding version; scan orders ≤ 200–300 for a counterexample.

**19. 16.95 (Thompson) — score 3.** Lines 4823–4826. Conjecture: for any A ∈ GL(n,F) there is a permutation matrix P with AP cyclic (minimal = characteristic polynomial).
Attack: exhaustive check over GL(n,q) for (n,q) ∈ {(3,2),(3,3),(4,2),(4,3),(5,2),(3,4),(3,5)} (|GL(4,3)|·24 ≈ 6·10^8 cheap tests in C). A counterexample over a small field refutes it instantly; otherwise evidence only.

**20. 15.75(b) (Plotkin) — score 3.** Lines 4245–4247. u_1 = [x,y], u_{n+1} = [[u_n,x],[u_n,y]]: is a finite group solvable iff it satisfies some identity u_n = 1? (The BGGKPP theorem uses a different sequence; this one is open.)
Attack: for minimal simple groups (L2(2^p), L2(3^p), L2(p), Sz(2^p), L3(3)) find x, y with u_n(x,y) ≠ 1 for all n — search fixed points u = [[u,x],[u,y]] ≠ 1 in L2(q) for small q with GAP, then push to all q by the BGGKPP algebraic-geometry/Lang–Weil method (Singular). Computational step is a day; the general argument a few more.

**21. 14.69(b),(c),(d) (Nuzhin) — score 3.** Lines 3564–3575. For each finite simple group, the minimal number of generating involutions that are (b) all conjugate; (c) conjugate with product 1; (d) conjugate with two commuting. (Part (a) is solved; Ward's thesis has partial results.)
Attack: for all ATLAS groups compute via class structure constants (`ClassMultiplicationCoefficient`) and Möbius-type counting whether 3 (for b), 4 (for c: three conjugate involutions with product 1 generate a dihedral group), 3 or 4 (for d) suffice; produces complete tables for sporadic groups and small Lie type. Full families need theory.

**22. 16.29 (Vdovin) — score 3.** Lines 4551–4558. Which simple groups of Lie type satisfy: for every semisimple abelian A and proper H there is x with A^x ∩ H = 1? (Exception L2(5), A = 2², H = 5:2.)
Attack: for L2(q), L3(q), U3(q), Sp4(q), G2(q) of order ≤ 10^7 enumerate abelian semisimple subgroups up to conjugacy and maximal subgroups, test by orbit computations; gives the complete list of small exceptions.

**23. 15.11 (Morigi) — score 3.** Lines 3833–3835. Is every finite abelian p-group the group of all power automorphisms Pot(G) of some group?
Attack: compute Pot(G) (automorphisms fixing every cyclic subgroup) for groups of order ≤ 500; collect which abelian p-groups occur (Pot(G×H) = Pot(G)×Pot(H) for coprime orders); then aim for a construction. Good exploratory computation, uncertain finish.

**24. 14.91 (Fernández-Alcober) — score 3.** Lines 3688–3689. Hall's formula k(P) = n(p²−1) + p^e + a(p²−1)(p−1) (|P| = p^{2n+e}) defines the abundance a. Do p-groups of every abundance a ≥ 0 exist?
Attack: compute abundance for all groups of order ≤ 3^8, 5^7, 7^7, 2^9 and look at the realized set; useful recursion: a(P×C_p) = ⌊m/2⌋ + p·a(P). Missing small values would sharpen the problem; a general family would settle it.

**25. 16.76 (Nuzhin) — score 3.** Lines 4744–4746. In which groups of Lie type in characteristic 2 is the maximal unipotent subgroup U strictly real (every nontrivial element inverted by an involution of U)?
Attack: GAP over small q and rank (`SylowSubgroup`, `IsConjugate` with involution witnesses) for A_n, B_n, D_n, G2, F4, ²B2, ²F4, ³D4; the pattern in q and type usually stabilizes quickly and can then be proved.

Lower-scored but noted (score 2): 16.3 (classes of distinct sizes ⇒ S3; only the nonsolvable case remains, theory-bound), 16.4 (Arad–Herzog; largely done by Guralnick–Malle–Tiep, remaining cases theoretical), 16.1(c) (commuting-graph isomorphism vs solvability; nauty search over orders ≤ 1000 is possible but counterexamples are unlikely small), 14.95 (class-breadth, p odd; small orders already scanned), 15.48 (SLP length < 2 log₂|G|; minimal SLP length is expensive to compute), 15.67 (three involutions, two commuting, for Sp_{2n}(Z), orthogonal groups, F4(Z); needs Nuzhin-style word searches), 16.53 (d(⟨A,B⟩) ≤ d+1; counterexamples would need large rank).

### Top 5

1. **16.60** — pure finite search over Aut G and character degrees; cheapest complete test with real chance of a counterexample.
2. **15.2(a)/(b)** — character-table scans (SmallGroups + CTblLib) give either a solvable counterexample or a full table of simple groups with nonvanishing elements.
3. **14.44** (with 14.74 as a free by-product) — exhaustive coprime-factorization search over all groups of order ≤ 2000 plus simple-group factorizations.
4. **15.74, case p = 5** — finite lattice computation (Arguesian test on normal-subgroup lattices of 5-groups of class 5) that would settle the first open prime.
