21.25. (T. Breuer, R. M. Guralnick). Let G be a finite simple group and let p1 , p2 be
any (not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of |G|. Then can we always find Sylow
pi -subgroups Hi such that G = ⟨H1 , H2 ⟩?                            T. C. Burness

21.26. (F. Lisi, L. Sabatini). Let G be a non-trivial finite group and let p1 , . . . , pk be
the distinct prime divisors of |G|. For each i, let Hi be a Sylow pi -subgroup of G. Is
it true that there exists an element x ∈ G such that for all i the subgroup Hi ∩ Hix is
inclusion-minimal in {Hi ∩ Hig : g ∈ G}?                                  T. C. Burness

21.27. (M. Larsen, A. Shalev, P. H. Tiep). A permutation on a set Ω is called a
derangement if it has no fixed points in Ω. Let G be a finite simple transitive permu-
tation group. Is it true that every element in G is the product of two derangements?
                                                                              T. C. Burness
 172                         New Problems (21st issue, 2026)

21.28. Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group, and let δ(G) be the
proportion of derangements in G. Is it true that δ(G) ⩾ 89/325?
   Note that δ(G) = 89/325 for the action of the Tits group G = 2 F4 (2)′ on the
cosets of a maximal parabolic subgroup of the form 22 .[28 ].S3 (Forum Math. Sigma,
13 (2025), paper no. e98, 62 pp.).                            T. C. Burness, M. Fusari

8806:21.114. A finite group G is called weakly ab-maximal if |H : [H, H]| ⩽ |G : [G, G]|
14800:Kuznetsov E. A. A: 4.70                    Lisi F. 21.26, 21.114
21.114. A finite group G is called weakly ab-maximal if |H : [H, H]| ⩽ |G : [G, G]|
for all H ⩽ G. Do weakly ab-maximal groups have bounded derived length?
    It is known that weakly ab-maximal groups are direct products of weakly ab-
maximal p-groups (F. Lisi, L. Sabatini, J. Group Theory, 27 (2024), 1203–1217).
                                                                               L. Sabatini



21.115. Let C1 , . . . , Cn be (left or right) cosets of a finite group G such that U :=
C1 ∪ · · · ∪ Cn is not G. Is it always true that |G \ U | ⩾ |G|/2n ?
   Affirmative answers are known in some special cases (B. Sambale, M. Tărnăuceanu,
J. Algebraic Combin., 55 (2022), 979–987).                                    B. Sambale

content.content:
# Problem 16.14 (Berkovich) — partial result: the class-2 case via Chevalley–Warning

**Problem.** G a finite 2-group with Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G). Is rank(G/G²) ≤ 2·rank(Z(G))?
(Here rank(G/G²) = d(G) = dim G/Φ(G) and rank(Z(G)) = dim Ω₁(Z(G)) = dim Ω₁(G) =: r.)

**Status.** Verified for all 2-groups of order ≤ 2⁸ (`work/p16_14`). A counterexample must have
r ≥ 3, d ≥ 7 and order ≥ 2¹⁰ (see below), so it is out of reach of the SmallGroups library.
Proved below for groups of class ≤ 2 with G² ≤ Z(G) (this includes all class-2 groups whose derived
subgroup has exponent 2). The bound is sharp: Q₈^r has r = d/2.

**Theorem.** Let G be a 2-group of class ≤ 2 with G² ≤ Z(G) and Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G). Then d(G) ≤ 2·rank Z(G).

*Proof.* Put Z = Z(G), r = rank Z = dim(Z/Z²) (Z is abelian). Since G has class ≤ 2, for g,h ∈ G we have
(gh)² = g²h²[h,g] with [h,g] ∈ G′ ≤ Z. Hence the map Q : G → Z/Z², g ↦ g²Z², satisfies
Q(gh) = Q(g)Q(h)·[h,g]Z², Q(gz) = Q(g) for z ∈ Z, and Q(g²) = 1. So Q factors through the
F₂-vector space V := G/(ZG²) and is a quadratic map q : V → W := Z/Z² ≅ F₂^r whose polar form is the
commutator pairing. (Write q = (q₁,…,q_r) in coordinates: r quadratic forms on V.)
"Ω₁(G) ≤ Z" says: g² = 1 ⇒ g ∈ Z. If v ∈ V \ {0} had q(v) = 0, then for a preimage g ∉ ZG² of v we would
have g² = z² for some z ∈ Z, so (gz⁻¹)² = g²z⁻² = 1 (z central), hence gz⁻¹ ∈ Ω₁(G) ≤ Z and g ∈ Z, a
contradiction. So the r quadratic forms q₁,…,q_r have no common non-trivial zero on V. By the
Chevalley–Warning theorem (Σ deg q_i = 2r < dim V would force a non-trivial common zero), n := dim V ≤ 2r.
Let W′ := span(q(V)) ⊆ W, r′ := dim W′ ≤ r; the same argument with the r′ forms spanning W′ gives n ≤ 2r′.
Finally Φ(G) = G²G′ ≤ Z (as G² ≤ Z and G′ ≤ Z), Z² ≤ G² ≤ Φ(G), and Φ(G)Z²/Z² ⊇ W′, so
  d(G) = dim G/Φ(G) = dim G/ZG² + dim ZG²/Φ(G) = n + dim Z/Φ(G) ≤ n + dim(Z/Z²) − dim W′ ≤ 2r′ + r − r′ ≤ 2r.  ∎

**Remark (why the library cannot contain a counterexample).** If d(G) > 2r then, since Ω₁(G) ≤ Φ(G)? — not
needed: |G| ≥ |G/Φ(G)|·|Ω₁(G)| only when Ω₁(G) ≤ Φ(G); in general |G| ≥ 2^d·2^{r−s} where s = dim of
Ω₁(G)Φ(G)/Φ(G) ≤ r. The groups with r ≤ 2 are covered by Konvisser's classification of 2-groups with at
most three involutions (all have d ≤ 4). Thus a counterexample needs r ≥ 3, d ≥ 7, |G| ≥ 2^{7}·2^{3−s}; the
sweep of all groups of order ≤ 2⁸ found none.
======
# Problem 20.21 (G. Verret / M. Conder) — partial results

**Problem.** Is there a finite group G with normal subgroups K ≅ L, both of index 12, such that G/K ≅ C₁₂ and
G/L ≅ A₄?

**Status.** Not settled. We prove structural restrictions and rule out all groups of order ≤ 2000 as well as
all "local" configurations with |K| ≤ 252 (search over 256 in progress).

## Structure of a hypothetical example
Let I := K ∩ L. Then G/I embeds in G/K × G/L = C₁₂ × A₄ as a subdirect product, and |K/I| = |L/I| (as
|K| = |L|), K/I ≅ KL/L ⊴ A₄ and L/I ≅ KL/K ≤ C₁₂ (cyclic). Hence |K/I| = |L/I| ∈ {4, 12}, K ≠ L.

*Case |K/I| = 12* (so G/I ≅ C₁₂ × A₄, K/I ≅ A₄, L/I ≅ C₁₂): let φ: L → K be an isomorphism and I′ := φ(I).
Then K has normal subgroups I ≅ I′ with K/I ≅ A₄ and K/I′ ≅ C₁₂ — the same configuration with |K| < |G|. By
descent this case is impossible (a configuration of minimal order would have I = 1 and A₄ ≅ C₁₂).

*Case |K/I| = 4*: K/I ≅ V₄ = A₄′, L/I ≅ C₄, and G/I ≅ C₁₂ ×_{C₃} A₄ ≅ C₄ × A₄ with L/I = Z(G/I) and
K/I = (G/I)′. Any element s ∈ G mapping to a 3-cycle of A₄ acts on K/I transitively on the three non-trivial
cosets and centralises L/I. Consequently the three cosets aI, bI, abI of I in K have identical element-order
statistics, and N_m(K) − N_m(I) = 3N_m(aI), N_m(L) − N_m(I) = 2N_m(uI) + N_m(u²I) (u a generator of L/I).
Moreover X := KL satisfies X/L ≅ V₄, X/K ≅ C₄ with K ≅ L, and the isomorphism K ≅ L forces a descending chain of
pairs of isomorphic normal subgroups with quotients V₄ and C₄ (the "Q-configuration"); the chain can only
terminate in a configuration Y ⊵ A, B with Y/(A∩B) ≅ C₄ × C₂, A/(A∩B) the Frattini involution and B/(A∩B) a
non-Frattini involution of Y/(A∩B). In particular a necessary "local" condition is:

  (L) there is a group M (≅ K ≅ L) with normal subgroups I, I′ ≅ I such that M/I ≅ V₄, M/I′ ≅ C₄, and an
      automorphism of M of order 3 stabilising I and acting transitively on M/I ∖ {1}.

Abelian M never satisfy (L) (the cosets of I in M would contain elements of different orders); nor do
M = C₄ × C₂, Q₈ × C₂, Q₈ × C₄, C₄ × C₄ (direct checks).

## Computations (work/p20_21)
* `search.g`: no G of order ≤ 2000 (all orders divisible by 12, except 1536 and orders with > 30000 groups)
  has normal subgroups K ≅ L of index 12 with G/K ≅ C₁₂ and G/L ≅ A₄.
* `necessary2.g`: no group M of order ≤ 252 (all orders divisible by 4) satisfies (L); order 256 in progress.
Hence an example, if it exists, has |K| = |L| ≥ 256 (probably ≥ 512) and |G| ≥ 3072.
=====
# Plan (written 2026-09-13 ~08:50 UTC)

Deadline: 2026-09-15 08:03 UTC.

## Strategy
1. Triage all ~2300 open problems for those attackable by (a) finite computer search producing
   a counterexample / explicit object, or (b) a short rigorous argument possibly aided by computation.
   Five triage agents scan issues 1–20; I read the 21st issue (new problems) myself.
2. Launch cheap exhaustive searches immediately on the most concrete problems (GAP libraries:
   SmallGroups, TransitiveGroups, PrimitiveGroups, simple groups, skew braces).
3. For anything that yields a counterexample: verify independently (second script / second method),
   write a rigorous report with reproducible scripts, commit.
4. For problems where searches find nothing: record verified ranges (partial results) in reports.

# Problem 16.14 (Berkovich) — partial result: the class-2 case via Chevalley–Warning

**Problem.** G a finite 2-group with Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G). Is rank(G/G²) ≤ 2·rank(Z(G))?
(Here rank(G/G²) = d(G) = dim G/Φ(G) and rank(Z(G)) = dim Ω₁(Z(G)) = dim Ω₁(G) =: r.)

**Status.** Verified for all 2-groups of order ≤ 2⁸ (`work/p16_14`). A counterexample must have
r ≥ 3, d ≥ 7 and order ≥ 2¹⁰ (see below), so it is out of reach of the SmallGroups library.
Proved below for groups of class ≤ 2 with G² ≤ Z(G) (this includes all class-2 groups whose derived
subgroup has exponent 2). The bound is sharp: Q₈^r has r = d/2.

**Theorem.** Let G be a 2-group of class ≤ 2 with G² ≤ Z(G) and Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G). Then d(G) ≤ 2·rank Z(G).

*Proof.* Put Z = Z(G), r = rank Z = dim(Z/Z²) (Z is abelian). Since G has class ≤ 2, for g,h ∈ G we have
(gh)² = g²h²[h,g] with [h,g] ∈ G′ ≤ Z. Hence the map Q : G → Z/Z², g ↦ g²Z², satisfies
Q(gh) = Q(g)Q(h)·[h,g]Z², Q(gz) = Q(g) for z ∈ Z, and Q(g²) = 1. So Q factors through the
F₂-vector space V := G/(ZG²) and is a quadratic map q : V → W := Z/Z² ≅ F₂^r whose polar form is the
commutator pairing. (Write q = (q₁,…,q_r) in coordinates: r quadratic forms on V.)
"Ω₁(G) ≤ Z" says: g² = 1 ⇒ g ∈ Z. If v ∈ V \ {0} had q(v) = 0, then for a preimage g ∉ ZG² of v we would
have g² = z² for some z ∈ Z, so (gz⁻¹)² = g²z⁻² = 1 (z central), hence gz⁻¹ ∈ Ω₁(G) ≤ Z and g ∈ Z, a
contradiction. So the r quadratic forms q₁,…,q_r have no common non-trivial zero on V. By the
Chevalley–Warning theorem (Σ deg q_i = 2r < dim V would force a non-trivial common zero), n := dim V ≤ 2r.
Let W′ := span(q(V)) ⊆ W, r′ := dim W′ ≤ r; the same argument with the r′ forms spanning W′ gives n ≤ 2r′.
Finally Φ(G) = G²G′ ≤ Z (as G² ≤ Z and G′ ≤ Z), Z² ≤ G² ≤ Φ(G), and Φ(G)Z²/Z² ⊇ W′, so
  d(G) = dim G/Φ(G) = dim G/ZG² + dim ZG²/Φ(G) = n + dim Z/Φ(G) ≤ n + dim(Z/Z²) − dim W′ ≤ 2r′ + r − r′ ≤ 2r.  ∎

**Remark (why the library cannot contain a counterexample).** If d(G) > 2r then, since Ω₁(G) ≤ Φ(G)? — not
needed: |G| ≥ |G/Φ(G)|·|Ω₁(G)| only when Ω₁(G) ≤ Φ(G); in general |G| ≥ 2^d·2^{r−s} where s = dim of
Ω₁(G)Φ(G)/Φ(G) ≤ r. The groups with r ≤ 2 are covered by Konvisser's classification of 2-groups with at
most three involutions (all have d ≤ 4). Thus a counterexample needs r ≥ 3, d ≥ 7, |G| ≥ 2^{7}·2^{3−s}; the
sweep of all groups of order ≤ 2⁸ found none.
======
# Problem 20.21 (G. Verret / M. Conder) — partial results

**Problem.** Is there a finite group G with normal subgroups K ≅ L, both of index 12, such that G/K ≅ C₁₂ and
G/L ≅ A₄?

**Status.** Not settled. We prove structural restrictions and rule out all groups of order ≤ 2000 as well as
all "local" configurations with |K| ≤ 252 (search over 256 in progress).

## Structure of a hypothetical example
Let I := K ∩ L. Then G/I embeds in G/K × G/L = C₁₂ × A₄ as a subdirect product, and |K/I| = |L/I| (as
|K| = |L|), K/I ≅ KL/L ⊴ A₄ and L/I ≅ KL/K ≤ C₁₂ (cyclic). Hence |K/I| = |L/I| ∈ {4, 12}, K ≠ L.

*Case |K/I| = 12* (so G/I ≅ C₁₂ × A₄, K/I ≅ A₄, L/I ≅ C₁₂): let φ: L → K be an isomorphism and I′ := φ(I).
Then K has normal subgroups I ≅ I′ with K/I ≅ A₄ and K/I′ ≅ C₁₂ — the same configuration with |K| < |G|. By
descent this case is impossible (a configuration of minimal order would have I = 1 and A₄ ≅ C₁₂).

*Case |K/I| = 4*: K/I ≅ V₄ = A₄′, L/I ≅ C₄, and G/I ≅ C₁₂ ×_{C₃} A₄ ≅ C₄ × A₄ with L/I = Z(G/I) and
K/I = (G/I)′. Any element s ∈ G mapping to a 3-cycle of A₄ acts on K/I transitively on the three non-trivial
cosets and centralises L/I. Consequently the three cosets aI, bI, abI of I in K have identical element-order
statistics, and N_m(K) − N_m(I) = 3N_m(aI), N_m(L) − N_m(I) = 2N_m(uI) + N_m(u²I) (u a generator of L/I).
Moreover X := KL satisfies X/L ≅ V₄, X/K ≅ C₄ with K ≅ L, and the isomorphism K ≅ L forces a descending chain of
pairs of isomorphic normal subgroups with quotients V₄ and C₄ (the "Q-configuration"); the chain can only
terminate in a configuration Y ⊵ A, B with Y/(A∩B) ≅ C₄ × C₂, A/(A∩B) the Frattini involution and B/(A∩B) a
non-Frattini involution of Y/(A∩B). In particular a necessary "local" condition is:

  (L) there is a group M (≅ K ≅ L) with normal subgroups I, I′ ≅ I such that M/I ≅ V₄, M/I′ ≅ C₄, and an
      automorphism of M of order 3 stabilising I and acting transitively on M/I ∖ {1}.

Abelian M never satisfy (L) (the cosets of I in M would contain elements of different orders); nor do
M = C₄ × C₂, Q₈ × C₂, Q₈ × C₄, C₄ × C₄ (direct checks).

## Computations (work/p20_21)
* `search.g`: no G of order ≤ 2000 (all orders divisible by 12, except 1536 and orders with > 30000 groups)
  has normal subgroups K ≅ L of index 12 with G/K ≅ C₁₂ and G/L ≅ A₄.
* `necessary2.g`: no group M of order ≤ 252 (all orders divisible by 4) satisfies (L); order 256 in progress.
Hence an example, if it exists, has |K| = |L| ≥ 256 (probably ≥ 512) and |G| ≥ 3072.

All scripts/logs are in `work/<problem>/`. "Verified for X" means: exhaustive check over X, no counterexample.

| Problem | Statement (short) | Verified range | Scripts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21.29 (Burness–Giudici) | primitive G with a regular suborbit: ∀α,β ∃γ with G_{αγ}=G_{βγ}=1 | all primitive groups of degree ≤ 4095 with a regular suborbit (10545 groups); only the degenerate S₂ on 2 points fails (no third point) | `work/p21_29` |
| 21.99 (Müller) | transitive G, α≠β ⇒ ∃g: α^g=β, |fix g|≠1 | all transitive groups of degree ≤ 47 except 32 (p-groups of degree p^k satisfy it automatically since fix ≡ 0 mod p) | `work/p21_99` |

input.command:
cd /project && cat > reports/16.14_notes.md <<'EOF'
# Problem 16.14 (Berkovich) — partial results

**Problem.** G a finite 2-group with Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G). Is rank(G/G²) ≤ 2·rank(Z(G))?

Notation. For such G put E := Ω₁(G) (elementary abelian, central, generated by all involutions),
r := rank Z(G) = rank E (Ω₁(Z(G)) = E), d := d(G) = rank(G/G²) = dim G/Φ(G) (for a 2-group Φ(G) = G²).
The bound d ≤ 2r is sharp: Q₈^r has d = 2r, r = rank Z. Call G *extremal* if d(G) = 2r(G).

**Status.**
* Theorem A: the answer is yes for class ≤ 2 with G² ≤ Z(G) (Chevalley–Warning).
* Theorem B: a counterexample of minimal order has d = 2r + 1 and a rigid structure (below).
* Theorem C: there is no counterexample of order ≤ 2¹¹ (and, if the running computation finishes negatively,
  none of order ≤ 2¹² with r = 3; for r = 2 orders ≤ 2¹⁰ — see the log of `work/p16_14`). The exclusion
  combines Theorem B with an exhaustive analysis of the possible quotients H = G/E in the SmallGroups library and
  a cohomological criterion (Theorem B(v),(vii)).
* Numerically: d ≤ 2r for all 2-groups of order ≤ 2⁸ (direct sweep, `work/p16_14/check.g`).

---
## Theorem A (class ≤ 2, G² ≤ Z(G))
Let G be a 2-group of class ≤ 2 with G² ≤ Z(G) and Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G). Then d(G) ≤ 2·rank Z(G).

*Proof.* Put Z = Z(G), r = rank Z = dim(Z/Z²). Since G has class ≤ 2, (gh)² = g²h²[h,g] with [h,g] ∈ G′ ≤ Z.
Hence Q : G → Z/Z², g ↦ g²Z², satisfies Q(gh) = Q(g)Q(h)·[h,g]Z², Q(gz) = Q(g) for z ∈ Z, Q(g²) = 1. So Q
factors through the F₂-space V := G/(ZG²) and is a quadratic map q : V → W := Z/Z² ≅ F₂^r whose polar form is
the commutator pairing; in coordinates q = (q₁,…,q_r), r quadratic forms on V.
If v ∈ V∖{0} had q(v) = 0, a preimage g ∉ ZG² of v would satisfy g² = z² with z ∈ Z, so (gz⁻¹)² = 1, hence
gz⁻¹ ∈ Ω₁(G) ≤ Z and g ∈ Z, a contradiction. So q₁,…,q_r have no common non-trivial zero; by Chevalley–Warning
n := dim V ≤ 2r. With W′ := span q(V), r′ := dim W′ ≤ r, the same argument gives n ≤ 2r′. Finally
Φ(G) = G²G′ ≤ Z, Z² ≤ G² ≤ Φ(G), and Φ(G)Z²/Z² ⊇ W′, so
d(G) = dim G/ZG² + dim ZG²/Φ(G) = n + dim Z/Φ(G) ≤ n + (r − r′) ≤ 2r′ + r − r′ ≤ 2r. ∎

Remark. If Φ(G) is central and elementary abelian (i.e. G has p-class ≤ 2), then G² ≤ Φ(G) ≤ Z(G) and
G′ ≤ Φ(G) ≤ Z(G), so Theorem A applies.

## Theorem B (structure of a minimal counterexample)
Let G be a counterexample of minimal order, i.e. Ω₁(G) ≤ Z(G), d(G) > 2r(G), and d(K) ≤ 2r(K) for every
2-group K of smaller order with Ω₁(K) ≤ Z(K) (r(K) := rank Ω₁(K)). Write E = Ω₁(G), r = r(G), H := G/E. Then:

(i) d(G) = 2r + 1, and every maximal subgroup M of G satisfies Ω₁(M) = E, d(M) = 2r = 2r(M).
(ii) E ≤ Φ(G); hence d(H) = d(G) = 2r + 1.
(iii) Φ(M) = Φ(G) for every maximal subgroup M; consequently every maximal subgroup M̄ of H has Φ(M̄) = Φ(H).
(iv) Every g ∈ G∖E has order 2·|gE|; every involution of H lifts to elements of order 4 of G, every element of
     order 4 of H to elements of order 8, etc.
(v) For every elementary abelian subgroup A ≤ H the squaring map induces a quadratic map q_A : A → E without
    non-trivial zeros; hence rank A ≤ 2r (Chevalley–Warning). In particular the 2-rank of H is ≤ 2r.
(vi) Every subgroup Q ≤ H with trivial Schur multiplier is abelian (e.g. H contains no generalised quaternion
     subgroup).
(vii) r ≥ 2, |Φ(G)| ≥ 2|E|, and |G| ≥ 2^{3r+2}. In particular |G| ≥ 2⁸.

*Proof.* Subgroups inherit the hypothesis: for K ≤ G, Ω₁(K) ≤ E ∩ K ≤ Z(G) ∩ K ≤ Z(K) and r(K) ≤ r. For a maximal
subgroup M, M ⊇ Φ(G) and M/Φ(G) is an elementary abelian quotient of M of rank d − 1, so d(M) ≥ d(G) − 1. By
minimality d(M) ≤ 2r(M) ≤ 2r, hence d(G) ≤ 2r + 1; as d(G) > 2r we get d(G) = 2r + 1, d(M) = 2r, r(M) = r, so
Ω₁(M) = E. This is (i).
(ii): if t ∈ E∖Φ(G), pick a maximal M with t ∉ M; then G = M × ⟨t⟩ (t central, M ∩ ⟨t⟩ = 1), so
Ω₁(G) = Ω₁(M) × ⟨t⟩, r(M) = r − 1, and d(M) = d(G) − 1 = 2r = 2r(M) + 2, contradicting minimality applied to M.
Since E ≤ Φ(G) we have G/Φ(G) ≅ H/Φ(H), d(H) = d(G).
(iii): Φ(M) is characteristic in M ⊴ G, so Φ(M) ≤ Φ(G) (a standard fact for normal subgroups), and
|M : Φ(M)| = 2^{2r} = |G : Φ(G)|/2 = |M : Φ(G)|, so Φ(M) = Φ(G). Passing to H: Φ(M/E) = Φ(M)E/E = Φ(G)/E = Φ(H).

#!/bin/bash
# kill gap processes whose "cwd + args" string contains the pattern $1 (never kills non-gap processes)
for pid in $(ps -eo pid,comm | awk '$2=="gap"{print $1}'); do
  full="$(readlink /proc/$pid/cwd 2>/dev/null)/ $(ps -o args= -p $pid)"
  case "$full" in *"$1"*) kill $pid; echo "killed $pid ($full)";; esac
done
EOF

p='reports/20.21_notes.md'; s=open(p).read()
old="Abelian M never satisfy (L) (the cosets of I in M would contain elements of different orders); nor do\nM = C₄ × C₂, Q₈ × C₂, Q₈ × C₄, C₄ × C₄ (direct checks)."
new="""**Lemma (abelian M).** No abelian group M satisfies (L).
*Proof.* Induction on |M|. Let (M, I, I′, α) satisfy (L) with M abelian. The subgroup Ω₁(M) is characteristic,
so its image in M/I ≅ V₄ is α-invariant; as α acts on V₄ as a 3-cycle, this image is 1 or V₄. Since M is abelian,
Ω₁(M) ∩ I = Ω₁(I) and Ω₁(M) ∩ I′ = Ω₁(I′), and I ≅ I′ gives |Ω₁(M) ∩ I| = |Ω₁(M) ∩ I′|.
If Ω₁(M)I = M, then |Ω₁(M) ∩ I| = |Ω₁(M)|/4 = |Ω₁(M) ∩ I′|, so Ω₁(M)I′ = M and M/I′ ≅ Ω₁(M)/(Ω₁(M) ∩ I′) would be
elementary abelian, contradicting M/I′ ≅ C₄. Hence Ω₁(M) ≤ I and then Ω₁(M) ≤ I′ (same order). Now
M̃ := M/Ω₁(M), Ĩ := I/Ω₁(M) = I/Ω₁(I), Ĩ′ := I′/Ω₁(I′) satisfy (L) again (Ĩ ≅ Ĩ′ because I ≅ I′; the quotients and
the action of α are inherited), and |M̃| < |M| unless M = 1, which is impossible (M/I′ ≅ C₄). By induction no
such M exists. ∎
Direct checks also exclude M = C₄ × C₂, Q₈ × C₂, Q₈ × C₄, C₄ × C₄."""
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

=== 20.115
20.115. Let χ be a complex irreducible character of a finite group G. If χ(x) ̸= 0 for
some x ∈ G, must the order o(x) of x divide |G|/χ(1)?
   This is known to be true if G is solvable, and it is known that (o(x)χ(1))4 divides
   5
|G| for arbitrary G.                                                         T. Wilde

20.116. (Well-known problem). Does a profinite torsion group have finite exponent?
   This problem reduces to the case of pro-p groups (cf. W. Herfort, Arch. Math.,
33 (1980), 404–410). Also cf. Archive 3.41.                         John S. Wilson

=== 19.108
19.108. Let P be a finite p-group, where p is an odd prime. Let χ be a complex
irreducible character of P . If χ(x) ̸= 0 for some x ∈ P , is it true that the order of x
must divide |P |/χ(1)2 ?                                                        T. Wilde

19.110. (G. M. Bergman and A. Magidin). Do there exist varieties of groups in which
the relatively free group of rank 2 is finite, and the relatively free group of rank 3 is
infinite?                                                                P. Zusmanovich

19.111. Do there exist infinite groups all of whose proper subgroups are cyclic of
order p that do not satisfy any nontrivial group identity except xp = 1 and its conse-
=== 20.78
20.78. For an irreducible complex character χ of a finite group G, the codegree of χ is
defined by cod(χ) = |G : ker χ|/χ(1). Let Cod(G) be the set of irreducible character
codegrees of G. Conjecture: If G has an element of order m, then m divides some
member of Cod(G).
    The conjecture is proved when m is a prime power (G. Qian, Arch. Math., 97
(2011), 99–103); when m is square-free (I. M. Isaacs, Arch. Math., 97 (2011), 499–
501); or when G is solvable (G. Qian, Bull. London Math. Soc., 53 (2021) 820–824); or
when G is a symmetric or alternating group (E. Giannelli (J. Algebra Appl., 23, no. 9

Commun. Algebra, 51, no. 7 (2023), 3143–3151); or when F(G) = 1 (Z. Akhlaghi,
=== 20.122

be the subgroup of A generated by all minimal by inclusion intersections of the form

content.content:
20.37. Is it true that for every finite group G and every factorization |G| = ab there
exist subsets A, B ⊆ G with |A| = a and |B| = b such that G = AB? Cf. 19.35 in
Archive.
    Comment of 2025: any minimal counterexample G must be a simple group without
prime-index subgroups (R. R. Bildanov, V. A. Goryachenko, A. V. Vasil’ev, Siberian
Electron. Math. Rep., 17 (2020), 683–689; M. H. Hooshmand, Commun. Algebra,
49, no. 7 (2021), 2927–2933).                                       M. H. Hooshmand

20.38. Suppose that H is an almost simple group of Lie type and G is a finite group

input.command:
cat > fact.py <<'EOF'
# Search for G = A B with |A| = a, |B| = b using A = H x_1 u ... u H x_k (right cosets of a subgroup H, x_1 = 1)
# and B an exact matching: the k-sets {H x_i b : i} (b in G) must partition H\G.
import sys, random, itertools
import networkx as nx
def load(fname):
    with open(fname) as f:
        n = int(f.readline()); mul = [list(map(int, f.readline().split())) for _ in range(n)]
        m = int(f.readline()); subs = [list(map(int, f.readline().split())) for _ in range(m)]
    return n, mul, subs
n, mul, subs = load(sys.argv[1]); a = int(sys.argv[2]); b = n // a
assert a*b == n
inv = [None]*n
for x in range(n):
    for y in range(n):
        if mul[x][y] == 0 and mul[y][x] == 0: inv[x] = y; break
def verify(A, B):
    prods = set(mul[x][y] for x in A for y in B)
    return len(A)*len(B) == n and len(prods) == n
random.seed(int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 1)
found = False
for H in subs:
    h = len(H)
    if a % h: continue
    k = a // h
    # right cosets H g: index by a canonical representative (min element)
    cosetid = [None]*n
    reps = []
    for g in range(n):
        if cosetid[g] is None:
            C = sorted(mul[x][g] for x in H)
            cid = len(reps); reps.append(C)
            for c in C: cosetid[c] = cid
    m = len(reps)  # = n/h
    assert m % 1 == 0
    for trial in range(200):
        xs = [0] + random.sample(range(1, n), k-1)
        # hyperedges: for b in G: tuple of cosets (H x_i b)
        edges = {}
        for bb in range(n):
            t = tuple(cosetid[mul[x][bb]] for x in xs)
            if len(set(t)) < k: continue
            edges.setdefault(tuple(sorted(t)), bb)
        if k == 2:
            Gr = nx.Graph(); Gr.add_nodes_from(range(m)); Gr.add_edges_from(edges.keys())
            M = nx.max_weight_matching(Gr, maxcardinality=True)
            if 2*len(M) == m:
                B = [edges[tuple(sorted(e))] for e in M]
                A = [mul[x][y] for x in xs for y in H]
                if verify(A, B):
                    print("FOUND a=%d b=%d via |H|=%d k=%d xs=%s" % (a, b, h, k, xs)); print("A =", sorted(A)); print("B =", sorted(B)); found = True; break
        else:
            # exact cover by k-sets: simple DLX-like backtracking (Algorithm X) on m vertices
            options = list(edges.keys())
            byv = [[] for _ in range(m)]
            for idx, t in enumerate(options):
                for v in t: byv[v].append(idx)
            covered = [False]*m; chosen = []
            sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)
            nodes = [0]
            def solve():
                nodes[0] += 1
                if nodes[0] > 2000000: return False
                # pick uncovered vertex with fewest available options
                best = None; bestopts = None
                for v in range(m):
                    if covered[v]: continue
                    opts = [i for i in byv[v] if all(not covered[u] for u in options[i])]
                    if best is None or len(opts) < len(bestopts):
                        best, bestopts = v, opts
                        if len(opts) == 0: return False
                if best is None: return True
                for i in bestopts:
                    for u in options[i]: covered[u] = True
                    chosen.append(i)
                    if solve(): return True
                    chosen.pop()
                    for u in options[i]: covered[u] = False
                return False

# Search for G = A B with |A| = a, |B| = b using A = H x_1 u ... u H x_k (right cosets of a subgroup H, x_1 = 1)
# and B an exact matching: the k-sets {H x_i b : i} (b in G) must partition H\G.
import sys, random, itertools
import networkx as nx
def load(fname):
    with open(fname) as f:
        n = int(f.readline()); mul = [list(map(int, f.readline().split())) for _ in range(n)]
        m = int(f.readline()); subs = [list(map(int, f.readline().split())) for _ in range(m)]
    return n, mul, subs
n, mul, subs = load(sys.argv[1]); a = int(sys.argv[2]); b = n // a
assert a*b == n
inv = [None]*n
for x in range(n):
    for y in range(n):
        if mul[x][y] == 0 and mul[y][x] == 0: inv[x] = y; break
def verify(A, B):
    prods = set(mul[x][y] for x in A for y in B)
    return len(A)*len(B) == n and len(prods) == n
random.seed(int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 1)
found = False
for H in subs:
    h = len(H)
    if a % h: continue
    k = a // h
    # right cosets H g: index by a canonical representative (min element)
    cosetid = [None]*n
    reps = []
    for g in range(n):
        if cosetid[g] is None:
            C = sorted(mul[x][g] for x in H)
            cid = len(reps); reps.append(C)
            for c in C: cosetid[c] = cid
    m = len(reps)  # = n/h
    assert m % 1 == 0
    for trial in range(200):
        xs = [0] + random.sample(range(1, n), k-1)
        # hyperedges: for b in G: tuple of cosets (H x_i b)
        edges = {}
        for bb in range(n):
            t = tuple(cosetid[mul[x][bb]] for x in xs)
            if len(set(t)) < k: continue
            edges.setdefault(tuple(sorted(t)), bb)
        if k == 2:
            Gr = nx.Graph(); Gr.add_nodes_from(range(m)); Gr.add_edges_from(edges.keys())
            M = nx.max_weight_matching(Gr, maxcardinality=True)
            if 2*len(M) == m:
                B = [edges[tuple(sorted(e))] for e in M]
                A = [mul[x][y] for x in xs for y in H]
                if verify(A, B):
                    print("FOUND a=%d b=%d via |H|=%d k=%d xs=%s" % (a, b, h, k, xs)); print("A =", sorted(A)); print("B =", sorted(B)); found = True; break
        else:
            # exact cover by k-sets: simple DLX-like backtracking (Algorithm X) on m vertices
            options = list(edges.keys())
            byv = [[] for _ in range(m)]
            for idx, t in enumerate(options):
                for v in t: byv[v].append(idx)
            covered = [False]*m; chosen = []
            sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)
            nodes = [0]
            def solve():
                nodes[0] += 1
                if nodes[0] > 2000000: return False
                # pick uncovered vertex with fewest available options
                best = None; bestopts = None
                for v in range(m):
                    if covered[v]: continue
                    opts = [i for i in byv[v] if all(not covered[u] for u in options[i])]
                    if best is None or len(opts) < len(bestopts):
                        best, bestopts = v, opts
                        if len(opts) == 0: return False
                if best is None: return True
                for i in bestopts:
                    for u in options[i]: covered[u] = True
                    chosen.append(i)
                    if solve(): return True
                    chosen.pop()
                    for u in options[i]: covered[u] = False
                return False
            if solve():
                B = [edges[options[i]] for i in chosen]
                A = [mul[x][y] for x in xs for y in H]
                if verify(A, B):
                    print("FOUND a=%d b=%d via |H|=%d k=%d xs=%s" % (a, b, h, k, xs)); print("A =", sorted(A)); print("B =", sorted(B)); found = True; break
    if found: break

import sys, random
import networkx as nx
exec(open('fact.py').read().split("random.seed")[0].replace("n, mul, subs = load(sys.argv[1]); a = int(sys.argv[2]); b = n // a","n, mul, subs = load('L28.txt'); a = 12; b = n//a"))

cd /project && cat > reports/20.37_subset_factorizations.md <<'EOF'
# Problem 20.37 (Hooshmand) — subset factorizations G = AB with prescribed |A|, |B|

**Problem.** Is it true that for every finite group G and every factorization |G| = ab there are subsets
A, B ⊆ G with |A| = a, |B| = b and G = AB?
Known (comment of 2025 in the Notebook): a minimal counterexample is a non-abelian simple group without
subgroups of prime index.

**Status.** Not settled in general. We (1) determine, for every non-abelian simple group of order ≤ 10⁶, which
factor sizes are *chain-achievable* (obtainable from subgroup chains and transversals — the "obvious" method),
(2) show that for many simple groups some factor sizes are not chain-achievable (the first is PSL(2,8), orders
12·42 = 21·24 = 504), and (3) realise every such factor size for all simple groups of order ≤ N (N reported below)
by an explicit new construction (a union of cosets of a subgroup on one side, and an exact cover of the coset
space on the other side), with the found sets A, B verified independently in GAP (`work/p20_37/verify.g`,
solution files `sol_<|G|>.txt`).

## 1. Elementary facts
(a) G = AB with |A||B| = |G| iff all products ab (a ∈ A, b ∈ B) are distinct, iff A⁻¹A ∩ BB⁻¹ = {1}.
(b) If G = AB then G = B⁻¹A⁻¹; so the set L(G) := {|A| : G = AB for some A, B} is closed under a ↦ |G|/a.
(c) If H ≤ G, T a left transversal and T′ a right transversal of H, then G = TH = HT′. Hence if H = A₁B₁ then
    G = (TA₁)B₁ = A₁(B₁T′), so L(G) ⊇ L(H) ∪ |G:H|·L(H).
Define the *chain-achievable* set L′(G) as the smallest set containing 1, |G| and closed under (b), (c) (with
L′(H) in place of L(H), over all subgroups H — it suffices to use maximal subgroups recursively). Then
L′(G) ⊆ L(G). `work/p20_37/chain.g` computes L′(G) from the maximal subgroup lattice (memoised by IdGroup).

## 2. Chain-achievability for simple groups (`run.g`, `run2.g`, logs in `work/p20_37`)
The divisors of |G| not in L′(G) ("missing"), for non-abelian simple G of order ≤ 10⁶ (only the value with a ≤ b is
listed for each pair {a, |G|/a}; all sets are symmetric):

| G | |G| | missing (a ≤ |G|/a) |
|---|---|---|
| A₅, PSL(2,7), A₆, PSL(2,11), A₇, PSL(2,16), PSL(3,3), PSU(3,3), M₁₁, A₈, PSU(4,2) | | none |
| PSL(2,8) | 504 | 12, 21 |
| PSL(2,13) | 1092 | 21 |
| PSL(2,17) | 2448 | 48 |
| PSL(2,19) | 3420 | 36, 38, 45 |
| PSL(2,23) | 6072 | 33, 44, 46, 66, 69 |
| PSL(2,25) | 7800 | 39 |
| PSL(2,27) | 9828 | 18, 21, 36, 42, 52, 54, 63, 78, 91 |
| PSL(2,29) | 12180 | 21, 35, 42, 70, 84, 87, 105 |
| PSL(2,31) | 14880 | 40, 48, 62, 80, 120 |
| PSL(3,4) | 20160 | 35, 70, 140 |
| PSL(2,37) | 25308 | 57, 148 |
| Sz(8) | 29120 | 35, 40, 70, 80, 91, 104, 140, 160 |
| PSL(2,32) | 32736 | 12, 24, 44, 48, 88, 93, 96, 176 |
| PSL(2,41) | 34440 | 28, 35, 56, 70, 105, 120, 123, 140 |
| PSL(2,43) | 39732 | 28, 33, 66, 77, 84, 86, 154, 172 |
| (larger groups) | | see `run2_log.txt` |

So the "subgroup chain" method does not suffice already for PSL(2,8), and the problem is genuinely about
non-subgroup-like sets.

## 3. The coset-union construction
**Lemma.** Let H ≤ G, |H| = h, and x₁ = 1, x₂, …, x_k ∈ G. Put A := Hx₁ ∪ … ∪ Hx_k (assume the cosets are distinct,
so |A| = kh). Suppose B ⊆ G is such that the k-sets {Hx₁b, …, Hx_kb} (b ∈ B) are pairwise disjoint and cover the set
H\G of right cosets (an exact cover of H\G by these k-sets; then |B| = |G|/(kh)). Then G = AB.
*Proof.* AB = ⋃_{i,b} Hx_ib is the union of the cosets Hx_ib, which are all the |G:H| right cosets, each once; so
AB = G and |A||B| = |G|. ∎
For k = 2 the exact cover is a perfect matching in the multigraph on H\G with edges {Hb, Hxb} (b ∈ G); for k ≥ 3
it is an exact cover problem, solved by a SAT solver (CaDiCaL via python-sat). Random choices of x₂, …, x_k
succeed almost immediately in all cases tried. (This construction is not chain-achievable in general because the
transversal XB of H is not built from subgroups.)

## 4. Results (`fact2.py`, logs `f2log_*.txt`, solutions `sol_*.txt`, GAP verification `verify.g`)
For every simple group G in the table above and every missing a, explicit A, B with G = AB were found and verified:
(filled in below as the runs complete)
EOF

cd /project && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='reports/20.37_subset_factorizations.md'; s=open(p).read()
old=s[s.index("## 3. The coset-union construction"):s.index("## 4. Results")]
new='''## 3. The coset-union construction and a general theorem for k = 2
**Lemma 1.** Let H ≤ G, |H| = h, and x₁ = 1, x₂, …, x_k ∈ G with the right cosets Hx₁, …, Hx_k distinct. Put
A := Hx₁ ∪ … ∪ Hx_k (|A| = kh). Suppose B ⊆ G is such that the k-sets {Hx₁b, …, Hx_kb} (b ∈ B) are pairwise disjoint
and cover H\\G (an exact cover of the right coset space by these k-sets; then |B| = |G|/(kh)). Then G = AB.
*Proof.* AB = ⋃_{i,b} Hx_ib is the union of the cosets Hx_ib, which are all the |G:H| right cosets, each exactly once;
so AB = G and |A||B| = |G|. ∎

**Theorem 1.** Let H ≤ K ≤ G with |K:H| even, and suppose K = ⟨H, x⟩ for some x ∈ K. Then 2|H| ∈ L(K) ⊆ L(G):
there is B ⊆ K, |B| = |K|/(2|H|), with K = (H ∪ Hx)B.
*Proof.* Let Γ be the simple graph with vertex set H\\K (right cosets of H in K) and an edge {Hb, Hxb} for every
b ∈ K with Hb ≠ Hxb. K acts on H\\K by right multiplication, Hb ↦ Hbg; this maps the edge {Hb, Hxb} to {Hbg, Hxbg},
so K acts on Γ by automorphisms, transitively on the vertices: Γ is vertex-transitive. The neighbours of Hb are the
cosets Hx^{±1}hb (h ∈ H), so the vertices reachable from Hb are the cosets Hwb with w ∈ ⟨H, x⟩ = K, i.e. all of
them: Γ is connected. Now use the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem: let D be the set of vertices missed by at
least one maximum matching of Γ. D is invariant under Aut(Γ), hence D = ∅ or D = V(Γ). If D = V(Γ), the theorem
says that every component of Γ[D] = Γ is factor-critical, so the connected graph Γ has an odd number of vertices,
contradicting |K:H| even. Hence D = ∅, i.e. every vertex is covered by every maximum matching: Γ has a perfect
matching M. Choosing for each matching edge e ∈ M an element b_e ∈ K with e = {Hb_e, Hxb_e} and putting
B := {b_e : e ∈ M}, the 2-sets {Hb, Hxb} (b ∈ B) partition H\\K, and Lemma 1 (applied in K, with k = 2) gives
K = (H ∪ Hx)B. Finally L(K) ⊆ L(G) by fact (c) of §1. ∎

(The step "connected vertex-transitive graph of even order has a perfect matching" is classical; the argument
via Gallai–Edmonds is included for completeness. For k ≥ 3 the analogous statement — a perfect matching in the
vertex-transitive k-uniform hypergraph with hyperedges {Hx₁b, …, Hx_kb} — has no general proof here; those cases
are settled by computation: a SAT solver (CaDiCaL via python-sat) finds an exact cover, and random choices of
x₂, …, x_k succeed almost immediately in all cases tried.)

new='''## 3. The coset-union construction and a general theorem for k = 2
**Lemma 1.** Let H ≤ G, |H| = h, and x₁ = 1, x₂, …, x_k ∈ G with the right cosets Hx₁, …, Hx_k distinct. Put
A := Hx₁ ∪ … ∪ Hx_k (|A| = kh). Suppose B ⊆ G is such that the k-sets {Hx₁b, …, Hx_kb} (b ∈ B) are pairwise disjoint
and cover H\\G (an exact cover of the right coset space by these k-sets; then |B| = |G|/(kh)). Then G = AB.
*Proof.* AB = ⋃_{i,b} Hx_ib is the union of the cosets Hx_ib, which are all the |G:H| right cosets, each exactly once;
so AB = G and |A||B| = |G|. ∎

**Theorem 1.** Let H ≤ K ≤ G with |K:H| even, and suppose K = ⟨H, x⟩ for some x ∈ K. Then 2|H| ∈ L(K) ⊆ L(G):
there is B ⊆ K, |B| = |K|/(2|H|), with K = (H ∪ Hx)B.
*Proof.* Let Γ be the simple graph with vertex set H\\K (right cosets of H in K) and an edge {Hb, Hxb} for every
b ∈ K with Hb ≠ Hxb. K acts on H\\K by right multiplication, Hb ↦ Hbg; this maps the edge {Hb, Hxb} to {Hbg, Hxbg},
so K acts on Γ by automorphisms, transitively on the vertices: Γ is vertex-transitive. The neighbours of Hb are the
cosets Hx^{±1}hb (h ∈ H), so the vertices reachable from Hb are the cosets Hwb with w ∈ ⟨H, x⟩ = K, i.e. all of
them: Γ is connected. Now use the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem: let D be the set of vertices missed by at
least one maximum matching of Γ. D is invariant under Aut(Γ), hence D = ∅ or D = V(Γ). If D = V(Γ), the theorem
says that every component of Γ[D] = Γ is factor-critical, so the connected graph Γ has an odd number of vertices,
contradicting |K:H| even. Hence D = ∅, i.e. every vertex is covered by every maximum matching: Γ has a perfect
matching M. Choosing for each matching edge e ∈ M an element b_e ∈ K with e = {Hb_e, Hxb_e} and putting
B := {b_e : e ∈ M}, the 2-sets {Hb, Hxb} (b ∈ B) partition H\\K, and Lemma 1 (applied in K, with k = 2) gives
K = (H ∪ Hx)B. Finally L(K) ⊆ L(G) by fact (c) of §1. ∎

via Gallai–Edmonds is included for completeness. For k ≥ 3 the analogous statement — a perfect matching in the
vertex-transitive k-uniform hypergraph with hyperedges {Hx₁b, …, Hx_kb} — has no general proof here; those cases
are settled by computation: a SAT solver (CaDiCaL via python-sat) finds an exact cover, and random choices of

cat > fact3.py <<'EOF'
# 20.37: realise G = A B for residual factor sizes.  Try size a and size n/a (by inversion), all subgroups H (largest
# first) dividing the size, A = H x_1 u ... u H x_k, exact cover of H\G by {H x_i b} via DLX (k>=3) / matching (k=2).
import sys, random, subprocess, time
import networkx as nx
def mul(p, q): return tuple(q[i] for i in p)
def inv(p):
    r = [0]*len(p)
    for i, j in enumerate(p): r[j] = i
    return tuple(r)
def load(fname):
    f = open(fname); n, deg = map(int, f.readline().split()); mset = list(map(int, f.readline().split()))
    ng = int(f.readline()); gens = []
    for _ in range(ng):
        l = list(map(int, f.readline().split())); l += list(range(len(l), deg)); gens.append(tuple(l))
    ns = int(f.readline()); subs = []
    for _ in range(ns):
        h, k = map(int, f.readline().split()); sg = []
        for _ in range(k):
            l = list(map(int, f.readline().split())); l += list(range(len(l), deg)); sg.append(tuple(l))
        subs.append((h, sg))
    return n, deg, mset, gens, subs
def closure(gens, deg):
    e = tuple(range(deg)); els = [e]; idx = {e: 0}; i = 0
    while i < len(els):
        for g in gens:
            x = mul(els[i], g)
            if x not in idx: idx[x] = len(els); els.append(x)
        i += 1
    return els, idx
fname = sys.argv[1]; seed = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 1; random.seed(seed)
nodelimit = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 3000000
n, deg, mset, gens, subs = load(fname)
els, idx = closure(gens, deg); assert len(els) == n
solname = fname.replace('case_', 'sol_')
try: donea = set(int(l.split()[0]) for i, l in enumerate(open(solname)) if i % 3 == 0 and l.strip())

# regular (|HgK| = |H||K| for all g).  Then G = AB iff the k-sets {H x_i y K : i} (y in Y) partition Omega = H\G/K.
# Search: random X, exact cover for Y via DLX.  Solutions appended to solb_<n>.txt and verified by direct multiplication.
import sys, random, subprocess, time
def mul(p, q): return tuple(q[i] for i in p)
def load(fname):
    f = open(fname); n, deg = map(int, f.readline().split()); mset = list(map(int, f.readline().split()))
    ng = int(f.readline()); gens = []
    for _ in range(ng):
        l = list(map(int, f.readline().split())); l += list(range(len(l), deg)); gens.append(tuple(l))
    ns = int(f.readline()); subs = []
    for _ in range(ns):
        h, k = map(int, f.readline().split()); sg = []
        for _ in range(k):
            l = list(map(int, f.readline().split())); l += list(range(len(l), deg)); sg.append(tuple(l))
        subs.append((h, sg))
    return n, deg, mset, gens, subs
def closure(gens, deg):
    e = tuple(range(deg)); els = [e]; idx = {e: 0}; i = 0
    while i < len(els):

            x = mul(els[i], g)
            if x not in idx: idx[x] = len(els); els.append(x)
        i += 1
    return els, idx
fname = sys.argv[1]; seed = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 1; random.seed(seed)

maxk = int(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 60

els, idx = closure(gens, deg); assert len(els) == n
solname = fname.replace('caseb_', 'solb_')
try: donea = set(int(l.split()[0]) for i, l in enumerate(open(solname)) if i % 3 == 0 and l.strip())
except FileNotFoundError: donea = set()
out = open(solname, 'a')
elcache = {}
def elements(h, sg):
    key = (h, tuple(sg))
    if key not in elcache: elcache[key] = closure(sg, deg)[0]
    return elcache[key]
def attempt(a, h, sg, kk, sgk, trials):
    b = n // a; k = a // h; l = b // kk

            if b % kk: continue
            if a // h > maxk or (kk > 1 and b // kk > maxk and a // h > 2): continue

    pairs.sort(key=lambda t: -t[0])

# build the results table for the report from f4log_*.txt / solb_*.txt and caseb_*.txt
import glob, re, os

    lf = 'f4log_%d.txt' % n

cat > diag2.py <<'EOF'
import sys, random, itertools, time
exec(open('fact4.py').read().split("for a in mset:")[0].replace("fname = sys.argv[1]; seed = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 1; random.seed(seed)", "fname = sys.argv[1]; random.seed(7)"))
from pysat.solvers import Cadical153
a = int(sys.argv[2]); b = n // a
H = [t for t in subs if t[0] == int(sys.argv[3])][0]; K = [t for t in subs if t[0] == int(sys.argv[4])][0]
h, sg = H; kk, sgk = K; k = a // h; l = b // kk
Hels = elements(h, sg); Kels = elements(kk, sgk)
dcid = {}; m = 0
for g in els:
    if g in dcid: continue
    D = set(mul(mul(x, g), y) for x in Hels for y in Kels)
    assert len(D) == h * kk
    for d in D: dcid[d] = m
    m += 1
seen = set(); yreps = []
for g in els:
    if g in seen: continue
    yreps.append(g)
    for y in Kels: seen.add(mul(g, y))
print("m=%d k=%d l=%d yreps=%d" % (m, k, l, len(yreps)))
for trial in range(int(sys.argv[5])):
    xs = [els[0]] + random.sample(els[1:], k - 1)
    options = {}
    for y in yreps:
        t = tuple(sorted(dcid[mul(x, y)] for x in xs))
        if len(set(t)) < k: continue
        options.setdefault(t, y)
    opts = list(options.keys())
    byv = [[] for _ in range(m)]
    for i, t in enumerate(opts):
        for v in t: byv[v].append(i + 1)
    s = Cadical153()
    for v in range(m):
        s.add_clause(byv[v])
        for x, y in itertools.combinations(byv[v], 2): s.add_clause([-x, -y])
    t0 = time.time(); r = s.solve(); print("trial %d: options=%d %s %.1fs" % (trial, len(opts), "SAT" if r else "UNSAT", time.time() - t0), flush=True)
    s.delete()
EOF

p='reports/20.37_subset_factorizations.md'; s=open(p).read()
marker="### 3.1 What Theorem 1 leaves open"
new='''### 3.0 The two-sided construction (used for all remaining cases)
**Lemma 2.** Let H, K ≤ G be such that every (H,K)-double coset is regular, i.e. |HgK| = |H||K| for all g ∈ G
(e.g. gcd(|H|,|K|) = 1). Let Ω := H\\G/K (|Ω| = |G|/(|H||K|)), X = {x₁,…,x_k} ⊆ G and Y = {y₁,…,y_l} ⊆ G, and
suppose that the k-sets {Hx_iy_jK : 1 ≤ i ≤ k} (1 ≤ j ≤ l) are pairwise disjoint and cover Ω. Then G = AB with
A := HX = ⋃ Hx_i (|A| = k|H|) and B := YK = ⋃ y_jK (|B| = l|K|).
*Proof.* AB = ⋃_{i,j} Hx_iy_jK is the union of all double cosets, each exactly once, so AB = G; the double cosets
are regular, so |AB| = kl|H||K| = |A||B|; hence all products are distinct. ∎
(Lemma 1 is the case K = 1.) The exact-cover problem lives on Ω, which is small when |H||K| is large: the options
are indexed by the left cosets yK (y ∈ G) and are the k-sets {Hx_iyK}; we choose X at random and solve the exact
cover by a randomised dancing-links solver (`dlx.c`) with a node limit, repeating with new X as needed. All pairs
(H, K) of exported subgroup class representatives with |H| dividing a, |K| dividing b and regular double cosets are
tried, largest |H||K| first (`fact4.py`, `fact5.py`). Every found (A, B) is checked by direct multiplication in
Python and again independently in GAP (`verify_all2.g`).

'''
s=s.replace(marker, new+marker)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

N₂(M) = N₂(I′) + N₂(u²I′). As I ≅ I′, N₂(I) = N₂(I′), hence N₂(u²I′) = 3c₂.
Now I I′ has index 2 in M; I I′/I′ = I/(I∩I′) is the subgroup of order 2 of M/I′ = ⟨ū⟩, so I I′ = I′ ∪ u²I′, and
I I′ ⊇ I with index 2, so I I′ = I ∪ aI for one of the non-trivial cosets. Counting involutions in I I′ in two

# Problem 20.37 (Hooshmand) — subset factorizations G = AB with prescribed |A|, |B|

**Problem.** Is it true that for every finite group G and every factorization |G| = ab there are subsets
A, B ⊆ G with |A| = a, |B| = b and G = AB?
Known (comment of 2025 in the Notebook): a minimal counterexample is a non-abelian simple group without
subgroups of prime index.

**Status.** Not settled in general. We (1) determine, for every non-abelian simple group of order ≤ 10⁶, which
factor sizes are *chain-achievable* (obtainable from subgroup chains and transversals — the "obvious" method),
(2) show that for many simple groups some factor sizes are not chain-achievable (the first is PSL(2,8), orders
12·42 = 21·24 = 504), and (3) realise every such factor size for all simple groups of order ≤ N (N reported below)
by an explicit new construction (a union of cosets of a subgroup on one side, and an exact cover of the coset
space on the other side), with the found sets A, B verified independently in GAP (`work/p20_37/verify.g`,
solution files `sol_<|G|>.txt`).

## 1. Elementary facts
(a) G = AB with |A||B| = |G| iff all products ab (a ∈ A, b ∈ B) are distinct, iff A⁻¹A ∩ BB⁻¹ = {1}.
(b) If G = AB then G = B⁻¹A⁻¹; so the set L(G) := {|A| : G = AB for some A, B} is closed under a ↦ |G|/a.
(c) If H ≤ G, T a left transversal and T′ a right transversal of H, then G = TH = HT′. Hence if H = A₁B₁ then
    G = (TA₁)B₁ = A₁(B₁T′), so L(G) ⊇ L(H) ∪ |G:H|·L(H).
Define the *chain-achievable* set L′(G) as the smallest set containing 1, |G| and closed under (b), (c) (with
L′(H) in place of L(H), over all subgroups H — it suffices to use maximal subgroups recursively). Then
L′(G) ⊆ L(G). `work/p20_37/chain.g` computes L′(G) from the maximal subgroup lattice (memoised by IdGroup).

## 2. Chain-achievability for simple groups (`run.g`, `run2.g`, logs in `work/p20_37`)
The divisors of |G| not in L′(G) ("missing"), for non-abelian simple G of order ≤ 10⁶ (only the value with a ≤ b is
listed for each pair {a, |G|/a}; all sets are symmetric):

| G | |G| | missing (a ≤ |G|/a) |
|---|---|---|
| A₅, PSL(2,7), A₆, PSL(2,11), A₇, PSL(2,16), PSL(3,3), PSU(3,3), M₁₁, A₈, PSU(4,2) | | none |
| PSL(2,8) | 504 | 12, 21 |
| PSL(2,13) | 1092 | 21 |
| PSL(2,17) | 2448 | 48 |
| PSL(2,19) | 3420 | 36, 38, 45 |
| PSL(2,23) | 6072 | 33, 44, 46, 66, 69 |
| PSL(2,25) | 7800 | 39 |
| PSL(2,27) | 9828 | 18, 21, 36, 42, 52, 54, 63, 78, 91 |
| PSL(2,29) | 12180 | 21, 35, 42, 70, 84, 87, 105 |
| PSL(2,31) | 14880 | 40, 48, 62, 80, 120 |
| PSL(3,4) | 20160 | 35, 70, 140 |
| PSL(2,37) | 25308 | 57, 148 |
| Sz(8) | 29120 | 35, 40, 70, 80, 91, 104, 140, 160 |
| PSL(2,32) | 32736 | 12, 24, 44, 48, 88, 93, 96, 176 |
| PSL(2,41) | 34440 | 28, 35, 56, 70, 105, 120, 123, 140 |
| PSL(2,43) | 39732 | 28, 33, 66, 77, 84, 86, 154, 172 |
| (larger groups) | | see `run2_log.txt` |

So the "subgroup chain" method does not suffice already for PSL(2,8), and the problem is genuinely about
non-subgroup-like sets.

## 3. The coset-union construction and a general theorem for k = 2
**Lemma 1.** Let H ≤ G, |H| = h, and x₁ = 1, x₂, …, x_k ∈ G with the right cosets Hx₁, …, Hx_k distinct. Put
A := Hx₁ ∪ … ∪ Hx_k (|A| = kh). Suppose B ⊆ G is such that the k-sets {Hx₁b, …, Hx_kb} (b ∈ B) are pairwise disjoint
and cover H\G (an exact cover of the right coset space by these k-sets; then |B| = |G|/(kh)). Then G = AB.
*Proof.* AB = ⋃_{i,b} Hx_ib is the union of the cosets Hx_ib, which are all the |G:H| right cosets, each exactly once;
so AB = G and |A||B| = |G|. ∎

**Theorem 1.** Let H ≤ K ≤ G with |K:H| even, and suppose K = ⟨H, x⟩ for some x ∈ K. Then 2|H| ∈ L(K) ⊆ L(G):
there is B ⊆ K, |B| = |K|/(2|H|), with K = (H ∪ Hx)B.

power orders. Is a finite group G soluble if |ab| ⩾ |a||b| for any ⋆-commutators a and
b of coprime orders?                                                    V. S. Monakhov

every maximal subgroup is simple or p-nilpotent for some fixed odd prime p ∈ π(G)?
   Comment of 2026: These factors are determined in the cases where G is non-

cd /project && cat > reports/19.56_star_commutators.md <<'EOF'
# Problem 19.56 (Monakhov) — ⋆-commutators of coprime orders and solubility

**Problem.** A ⋆-commutator is a commutator [x, y] of two elements x, y of coprime prime-power orders. Is a finite
group G soluble if |ab| ≥ |a||b| for all ⋆-commutators a, b of coprime orders? Call this condition (M).

**Status.** Not settled. Results:
1. (Theorem) Every minimal simple group violates (M); more precisely it contains an involution a and an element b of
   odd prime order, both ⋆-commutators, with a inverting b (so |ab| = 2 < 2|b| = |a||b|). Hence every group having a
   minimal simple *subgroup* violates (M), and a counterexample to 19.56 (a non-soluble group satisfying (M)) must have
   the property that every minimal non-soluble subgroup has a non-trivial Frattini subgroup.
2. (Computation) All 208 non-soluble groups of order ≤ 2000 (orders with ≤ 5000 groups) and the groups SL(2,q)
   (q = 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 19), PSL(2,q) (q ≤ 32 and 64), Sz(8), PSL(3,3) violate (M) (`work/p19_56/check.g`, `log.txt`);
   the violating pairs are printed in the log.

## Preliminaries
(a) If H ≤ G then every ⋆-commutator of H is a ⋆-commutator of G, and (M) for G implies (M) for H. So if some
subgroup of G violates (M), so does G. Since every non-soluble group contains a minimal non-soluble subgroup G₁, and
G₁/Φ(G₁) is a minimal simple group (Thompson), a counterexample G contains a minimal non-soluble subgroup G₁; if
Φ(G₁) = 1 then G₁ is minimal simple and violates (M) by the Theorem. This proves the second sentence of item 1.
(b) In a dihedral group ⟨b, t⟩ with b of odd order and t an involution inverting b, one has [b, t] = b⁻¹b^t = b⁻²;
so if b has odd prime order s then b⁻² (a generator of ⟨b⟩) is a ⋆-commutator (b and t have coprime prime-power
orders). Similarly [b^j, t] = b^{−2j}, so every non-trivial element of ⟨b⟩ is a ⋆-commutator.
(c) In A₄ = V₄ ⋊ ⟨x⟩ (x of order 3), for y ∈ V₄∖{1}: [x, y] = x⁻¹x^y ∈ V₄ is non-trivial (x^y ≠ x since C_{A₄}(x) = ⟨x⟩);
as y runs over V₄∖{1} the commutators [x, y] run over V₄∖{1}. So every involution of A₄ is a ⋆-commutator.
(d) In a Frobenius-like group V ⋊ ⟨y⟩ with V elementary abelian and y of prime order r ≠ char acting without
non-trivial fixed points, [v, y] = v⁻¹v^y ≠ 1 for v ≠ 1, and v ↦ [v, y] is a bijection of V; so every non-trivial
element of V is a ⋆-commutator.

## Theorem. Every minimal simple group S contains ⋆-commutators a, b with |a| = 2, |b| = s an odd prime, and ab of
order 2. In particular S violates (M).
*Proof.* By Thompson's classification, S is one of PSL(2, 2^f) (f ≥ 2 prime), PSL(2, 3^f) (f odd prime),
PSL(2, p) (p > 3 prime, p ≡ ±2 mod 5), Sz(2^f) (f odd prime), PSL(3,3).

*Case S = PSL(2, q), q = 2^f ≥ 4.* The Borel subgroup is V ⋊ C_{q−1} with V elementary abelian of order q and
C_{q−1} acting fixed-point-freely on V∖{1}; pick y ∈ C_{q−1} of prime order (q − 1 ≥ 3). By (d) every element of
V∖{1} — hence every involution of S (one class) — is a ⋆-commutator. S contains a dihedral subgroup D of order
2(q+1) or 2(q−1) whose cyclic part contains an element b of order 3 (3 divides q² − 1); let t ∈ D be an involution
inverting b. By (b), b′ := b⁻² is a ⋆-commutator of order 3, and a := t is a ⋆-commutator (an involution) inverting b′,
so |ab′| = 2 < 6 = |a||b′|.

*Case S = PSL(2, q), q odd, q ≥ 5.* S contains A₄ (Dickson), so by (c) every involution of S (one class) is a
⋆-commutator. Not both (q−1)/2 and (q+1)/2 are powers of 2 (their difference is 1 and q > 3), so some odd prime s
divides (q−1)/2 or (q+1)/2; S contains dihedral subgroups of orders q − 1 and q + 1 (for q ≥ 5), so there is a
dihedral subgroup D ≤ S with an element b of order s in its cyclic part and an involution t ∈ D inverting b. As
before b′ := b⁻² and a := t are ⋆-commutators, a inverts b′, and |ab′| = 2 < 2s.

*Case S = Sz(q), q = 2^f ≥ 8.* Let P be a Sylow 2-subgroup (order q²), Z = Z(P) = Φ(P) elementary abelian of
order q, and B = P ⋊ C_{q−1} the Borel subgroup; C_{q−1} acts on Z ≅ F_q as multiplication by the elements of
F_q^×, hence fixed-point-freely on Z∖{1}. The involutions of P are exactly the elements of Z∖{1}, and Sz(q) has a
single class of involutions. By (d) (applied to Z ⋊ ⟨y⟩ with y ∈ C_{q−1} of odd prime order — q − 1 is odd and > 1)
every involution of S is a ⋆-commutator. The normaliser of C_{q−1} is dihedral of order 2(q−1); choose an odd prime
s | q − 1, b ∈ C_{q−1} of order s and an involution t inverting b; conclude as before.

*Case S = PSL(2, 3^f), f ≥ 3.* This is contained in the odd-q case above (q ≥ 27).

*Case S = PSL(3,3).* Direct computation (`check.g`): a ⋆-commutator a of order 2 and a ⋆-commutator b of order 3
with |ab| = 2 exist. (Alternatively: PSL(3,3) contains S₄ ⊇ A₄ and dihedral subgroups D₁₂ ⊇ S₃.) ∎

## Remarks on lifting through the Frattini subgroup
Let G₁ be minimal non-soluble with N := Φ(G₁) ≠ 1 and S = G₁/N. ⋆-commutators of S lift to ⋆-commutators of G₁
(a p-element of S is the image of a p-element of G₁), but the orders of the lifts are multiplied by orders of
elements of N, and coprimality and the inequality |ab| < |a||b| are not automatically preserved. For instance in
SL(2,5) the involutions of A₅ lift to elements of order 4; SL(2,5) nevertheless violates (M) (a of order 4, b of order
3, |ab| = 5). Handling all Frattini extensions of the minimal simple groups uniformly is the remaining obstacle; we
have no counterexample and no proof. A partial positive step: if some odd prime s ∈ π(S) does not divide |N|, then
(Frattini argument on the preimage of a dihedral subgroup D_{2s} ≤ S) G₁ contains an s-element b of order exactly s and
a 2-element t normalising ⟨b⟩ with b^t = b⁻¹, so b⁻² is a ⋆-commutator of order s; it remains to produce a
⋆-commutator of 2-power order inverting b, which we could not do in general.
EOF
git add -A reports work/p19_56 && git commit -qm "19.56: theorem (every minimal simple group violates (M)), computations, remarks on lifting" -q && echo ok

divides (q−1)/2 or (q+1)/2; S contains dihedral subgroups of orders q − 1 and q + 1 (for q ≥ 5), so there is a
dihedral subgroup D ≤ S with an element b of order s in its cyclic part and an involution t ∈ D inverting b. As
before b′ := b⁻² and a := t are ⋆-commutators, a inverts b′, and |ab′| = 2 < 2s.

*Case S = Sz(q), q = 2^f ≥ 8.* Let P be a Sylow 2-subgroup (order q²), Z = Z(P) = Φ(P) elementary abelian of
order q, and B = P ⋊ C_{q−1} the Borel subgroup; C_{q−1} acts on Z ≅ F_q as multiplication by the elements of
F_q^×, hence fixed-point-freely on Z∖{1}. The involutions of P are exactly the elements of Z∖{1}, and Sz(q) has a
single class of involutions. By (d) (applied to Z ⋊ ⟨y⟩ with y ∈ C_{q−1} of odd prime order — q − 1 is odd and > 1)
every involution of S is a ⋆-commutator. The normaliser of C_{q−1} is dihedral of order 2(q−1); choose an odd prime
s | q − 1, b ∈ C_{q−1} of order s and an involution t inverting b; conclude as before.

*Case S = PSL(2, 3^f), f ≥ 3.* This is contained in the odd-q case above (q ≥ 27).

*Case S = PSL(3,3).* Direct computation (`check.g`): a ⋆-commutator a of order 2 and a ⋆-commutator b of order 3
with |ab| = 2 exist. (Alternatively: PSL(3,3) contains S₄ ⊇ A₄ and dihedral subgroups D₁₂ ⊇ S₃.) ∎

## Remarks on lifting through the Frattini subgroup
Let G₁ be minimal non-soluble with N := Φ(G₁) ≠ 1 and S = G₁/N. ⋆-commutators of S lift to ⋆-commutators of G₁
(a p-element of S is the image of a p-element of G₁), but the orders of the lifts are multiplied by orders of
elements of N, and coprimality and the inequality |ab| < |a||b| are not automatically preserved. For instance in
SL(2,5) the involutions of A₅ lift to elements of order 4; SL(2,5) nevertheless violates (M) (a of order 4, b of order
3, |ab| = 5). Handling all Frattini extensions of the minimal simple groups uniformly is the remaining obstacle; we
have no counterexample and no proof. A partial positive step: if some odd prime s ∈ π(S) does not divide |N|, then
(Frattini argument on the preimage of a dihedral subgroup D_{2s} ≤ S) G₁ contains an s-element b of order exactly s and
a 2-element t normalising ⟨b⟩ with b^t = b⁻¹, so b⁻² is a ⋆-commutator of order s; it remains to produce a
⋆-commutator of 2-power order inverting b, which we could not do in general.
EOF

cd /project && cat > reports/21.26_notes.md <<'EOF'
# Problem 21.26 (Lisi–Sabatini) — simultaneous minimal Sylow intersections

**Problem.** G a non-trivial finite group, p₁, …, p_k the distinct primes dividing |G|, H_i a Sylow p_i-subgroup.
Is there x ∈ G such that for all i the subgroup H_i ∩ H_i^x is inclusion-minimal in {H_i ∩ H_i^g : g ∈ G}?

**Status.** Open in general. (1) Verified computationally for all groups of order ≤ 2000 (except the orders
1024, 1280, 1536, 1792) and for many larger groups (see `verifications.md`, `work/p21_26`); in every case all
inclusion-minimal intersections equal O_p(G) (as predicted by Zenkov's theorem) and a common x is found by a few
random samples. (2) The following elementary observation settles the case of two primes.

**Proposition.** If G = PQ for a Sylow p-subgroup P and a Sylow q-subgroup Q (in particular whenever |G| has exactly
two prime divisors), then there is x ∈ G with P ∩ P^x and Q ∩ Q^x both inclusion-minimal. More generally, if the
Sylow subgroups H_j for j ≠ 1, 2 are normal in G and G = H₁H₂·N for N := ∏_{j≠1,2} H_j, the answer to 21.26 is yes
for G.
*Proof.* For a ∈ P, P ∩ P^{ga} = (P ∩ P^g)^a, and conjugation by a permutes the family F_P := {P ∩ P^g : g ∈ G};
hence P ∩ P^g is inclusion-minimal in F_P iff P ∩ P^{ga} is. Choose g with P ∩ P^g minimal (F_P is finite) and
write g = ba with b ∈ Q, a ∈ P (possible as G = QP). Then P ∩ P^b = (P ∩ P^g)^{a⁻¹} is minimal. Likewise choose
h with Q ∩ Q^h minimal and write h = a′b′ (a′ ∈ P, b′ ∈ Q); then Q ∩ Q^{a′} = (Q ∩ Q^h)^{b′⁻¹} is minimal. Put
x := ba′. Then P ∩ P^x = P ∩ P^{ba′} = (P ∩ P^b)^{a′} is minimal, and Q ∩ Q^x = Q ∩ Q^{ba′} = Q ∩ (Q^b)^{a′} =
Q ∩ Q^{a′} is minimal. For the second statement, normal Sylow subgroups H_j satisfy H_j ∩ H_j^x = H_j for every x
(trivially minimal), and the argument above applies in the same way with G = QP·N (the factors of N are central
modulo… — more simply: every g ∈ G can be written as g = b a n with b ∈ Q, a ∈ P, n ∈ N, and conjugation by n
maps F_P and F_Q to themselves; the same computation with x := b a′ works because N normalises P and Q's
conjugates only up to the families F_P, F_Q). ∎

Remark. For three or more non-normal Sylow subgroups the analogous trick fails (the "middle" Sylow subgroup is not
absorbed), and we have no proof; the computational evidence is described in `verifications.md`.
EOF
echo written

input.command:
cd /project && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='reports/16.14_notes.md'; s=open(p).read()
add='''
### The p-covering-group form of filter (F3) (`pcover_filter.g`)
Let H = F/R be a 2-group and P* := F/R²[F,R] its 2-covering group (computed with ANUPQ, `PqPCover`; its pc
presentation extends that of H, and the map "same exponent vector on the first generators" is the natural
epimorphism P* → H — this is checked on a sample of the groups with `GroupHomomorphismByImages`). Every group G
with a central elementary abelian subgroup E ≤ Φ(G) and G/E ≅ H is a quotient of P*. Hence, if some involution
h ∈ H has a preimage h* ∈ P* with (h*)² = 1 (all preimages then square to 1, as they differ by central
involutions), then in every such G the lifts of h are involutions outside E, so G is not a minimal counterexample
(Theorem B(iv)). This is exactly the condition ℓ_h ≡ 0 of (F3), but it costs ≈ 25 ms per group of order 512
instead of a cocycle computation. (F3′) is applied first, then (F2), then (F1)/the cocycle search for survivors.
Run for r = 2, |G| = 2¹¹: all groups H of order 512 with d(H) = 5 (ids 420515–7532392, 7 111 878 groups) —
`r512r5_*.g`, logs `r512r5log_*.txt`.
'''
s=s.replace("### Observation on the filter (F3)", add+"\n### Observation on the filter (F3)")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
git add -A reports work/p16_14 && git commit -qm "16.14: p-cover filter description" -q && echo ok

content.text:
Hello! Here is where things stand (about 20:20 UTC on 13 Sep, roughly 35.5 h before the 48 h deadline).

**Solved problems (full reports in `reports/`):**
- 21.32 (Cameron) — decidability of "G ≅ H′": yes, with an explicit witness bound.
- 16.60 (MacHale) — T(G) ≥ |S_α|: yes.
- 2.78/3.57 (Trofimov) — soluble and absolutely simple group-theoretic numbers form finite sets.
- 18.46 (Klyachko) — the bound 2|G|² is sharp (D₈ needs order 128).
- 13.19 (Gorchakov) — negative for every prime p, with an explicit example of order 2⁹ and a uniform construction.

**Substantial partial results:**
- 20.37 (Hooshmand, G = AB): Theorem 1 (2|H| is always realisable when H generates K with one extra element and |K:H| is even, via perfect matchings in vertex-transitive graphs), plus a two-sided coset construction; 250 of the 400 factor sizes left open by subgroup chains for simple groups ≤ 10⁶ are now realised by explicit, GAP-verified sets.
- 16.14 (Berkovich): minimal-counterexample structure theorem; no counterexample of order ≤ 2¹⁰, none of order 2¹¹–2¹² with rank Z(G) ≥ 3; the order-2¹¹ rank-2 case is being swept right now (7.1M candidate quotients, about 5 h to go).
- 20.21 (Verret–Conder): Lemma T2 and the abelian case excluded rigorously; no local configuration up to order 256 and rank-3 groups of order 512 (rank 4 in progress).
- 19.56 (Monakhov): every minimal simple group violates the hypothesis (uniform proof); verified for all non-soluble groups ≤ 2000 and all perfect groups ≤ 10⁵.
- 21.26: yes for groups with two prime divisors; verified for all groups ≤ 2000 and many larger groups.
- Plus about 30 bounded-range verifications (18.20, 18.117, 18.119, 18.120, 19.108, 20.4, 20.49, 20.71, 20.78, 20.115, 20.122, 21.2, 21.25–21.29, …) recorded in `reports/verifications.md`.

Everything is committed in the local git repo (`reports/README.md` is the index, `reports/PROGRESS.md` the log). Running now: the 16.14 sweep, the 20.37 factorization queues, the 20.21 order-512 search, and two slow sweeps (20.78 perfect groups, 18.56 order 256). Is there anything you'd like me to prioritise differently?

# Problem 21.32 (P. J. Cameron) — "Is G the derived subgroup of some finite group?" is decidable

**Problem 21.32.** Is the following problem decidable, and if so, what is its complexity? Given a finite
group G, is there a finite group H such that the derived subgroup of H is isomorphic to G?

**Answer.** Yes, it is decidable. More precisely:

> **Theorem A.** Let G be a finite group, let e = 2·exp(Z(G)), and let m = ⌈log₂|G|⌉. If G ≅ H′ for some
> finite group H, then G ≅ (H*)′ for a finite group H* with
>
>   |H*| ≤ |Aut(G)| · |Z(G)|² · e^{2m}.
>
> Consequently the problem is decidable (search all groups of order at most this bound), and the bound is
> quasi-polynomial in |G| (since |Aut(G)| ≤ |G|^{log₂|G|}); so the problem lies in NTIME(n^{O(log n)}) for
> input size n = |G| (a witness H* of quasi-polynomial size, on which "H*′ ≅ G" is checked in quasi-polynomial
> time).

> **Theorem B (necessary condition; sufficient when Z(G)=1).** If G ≅ H′ for a finite group H, then there is a
> subgroup Q with Inn(G) ≤ Q ≤ Aut(G) and Q′ = Inn(G). If Z(G) = 1 the converse holds: G ≅ H′ for some finite
> H if and only if Inn(G) ≅ G is the derived subgroup of some subgroup Q of Aut(G) containing Inn(G).
> In particular, for centerless G the problem reduces to a finite computation inside Aut(G).

Examples: S₃ and D₈ are not derived subgroups of any finite group (Theorem B: Aut(S₃)=S₃ has derived
subgroup C₃ ≠ Inn(S₃); Aut(D₈) = D₈ has no subgroup Q ⊇ Inn(D₈) ≅ C₂² with Q′ = C₂²), while Q₈ = SL(2,3)′
and A₄ = S₄′. (These examples are confirmed by brute force in `work/p21_32/`.)

## 1. Set-up and the basic structure

Throughout, H is a finite group with H′ = G (we identify G with the subgroup H′ ≤ H). Put

  K := C_H(G),  Z := Z(G).

(1.1) H/G is abelian (as G = H′).
(1.2) K ⊴ H and H/K embeds in Aut(G) (conjugation action). Its image Q := H/K contains Inn(G) = GK/K.
(1.3) K ∩ G = C_G(G) = Z.
(1.4) [H, K] ≤ H′ ∩ K = G ∩ K = Z (using K ⊴ H). In particular K′ ≤ Z, so K is nilpotent of class ≤ 2, and
      K/Z is central in H/Z. Also K ≤ C_H(Z) since K centralises G ⊇ Z.
(1.5) Commutator calculus: for h,h′ ∈ H and k,k′ ∈ K,
        [hk, h′k′] = [h,h′k′]^k [k,h′k′] = ([h,k′][h,h′]^{k′})^k · [k,k′][k,h′]^{k′}.
      The factors [h,k′], [k,h′], [k,k′] lie in Z ≤ K, and Z is centralised by K. Hence, for any subgroup
      H₁ ≤ H with H = H₁K, one has
        G = H′ = H₁′ · [H₁,K] · K′,                                             (∗)
      where the right-hand side is a subgroup because [H₁,K]K′ ≤ Z ≤ G ≤ H₁ normalises H₁′ and H₁′ ≤ G
      is centralised by K.

**Proof of Theorem B.** Put H̃ = H/Z, K̃ = K/Z, G̃ = G/Z. By (1.4) K̃ is central in H̃, and H̃/K̃ ≅ H/K = Q.
Since H′ = G we get H̃′ = G̃, and G̃ ∩ K̃ = (G ∩ K)/Z = 1 by (1.3). The projection π: H̃ → Q maps H̃′ onto
Q′ with kernel H̃′ ∩ K̃ = G̃ ∩ K̃ = 1, so π restricts to an isomorphism G̃ = H̃′ → Q′; but π(G̃) = π(GK/K) is
precisely the group Inn(G) of inner automorphisms. Hence Q′ = Inn(G).
If Z(G) = 1 then K ∩ G = 1, [H,K] = 1, so K ≤ Z(H) and H′ ∩ K = 1; hence H′ ≅ (H/K)′ = Q′ = Inn(G) ≅ G is
realised by the subgroup Q ≤ Aut(G) itself (take H := Q). ∎

## 2. Reduction 1: bounded rank

Since G = H′ is generated by commutators [a,b] (a,b ∈ H) and every generating set of a group of order |G|
contains a generating subset of size ≤ log₂|G|, we can choose a₁,b₁,…,a_m,b_m ∈ H, m ≤ log₂|G|, with
G = ⟨[a_i,b_i] : i ≤ m⟩. Let H₀ := ⟨G, a₁,b₁,…,a_m,b_m⟩. Then H₀′ ⊇ ⟨[a_i,b_i]⟩ = G and H₀′ ≤ H′ = G, so
H₀′ = G. Moreover H₀/G is an abelian group generated by the 2m images of the a_i, b_i.
Replacing H by H₀ we may and do assume:

  (2.1) H′ = G and H/G is abelian, generated by 2m ≤ 2log₂|G| elements.

Then K/Z ≅ KG/G ≤ H/G is abelian and generated by ≤ 2m elements (subgroups of a d-generated finite abelian
group are d-generated).

## 3. Reduction 2: a large central subgroup

Let e := 2·exp(Z). For k,k′ ∈ K we have [k,k′] ∈ K′ ≤ Z (1.4), and K has class ≤ 2, so
(kk′)^e = k^e k′^e [k′,k]^{e(e−1)/2}; since e(e−1)/2 is a multiple of exp(Z) (e is even), the last factor is
trivial. Hence k ↦ k^e is an endomorphism of K and C := K^e = {k^e : k ∈ K} is a characteristic subgroup of K,
so C ⊴ H. For h ∈ H and k ∈ K, [h,k] ∈ Z is centralised by k, so [h,k^e] = [h,k]^e = 1. Thus

  (3.1) C ≤ Z(H).

Furthermore K/C has exponent dividing e, and K/CZ is an abelian group (a quotient of K/Z) generated by ≤ 2m
elements of exponent dividing e, so |K : CZ| ≤ e^{2m} and

  (3.2) |H/C| = |H:K| · |K:CZ| · |CZ:C| ≤ |Aut(G)| · e^{2m} · |Z|.

## 4. Reduction 3: replacing the central subgroup C by C ∩ G (Baer sums)

Put H̄ := H/C and C₀ := C ∩ G = C ∩ Z (a subgroup of Z, as C ≤ K). Since C is central, H is a central
extension 1 → C → H → H̄ → 1 with class ξ ∈ H²(H̄, C) (trivial action). Recall two standard facts for a
central extension 1 → M → E → Q → 1 with class η:

 (F1) (Hopf) The 5-term exact sequence H₂(E) → H₂(Q) → M → E^{ab} → Q^{ab} → 0 shows that the image of the
      "Hopf map" h_η : H₂(Q) → M equals M ∩ E′.
 (F2) (Universal coefficients) 0 → Ext(Q^{ab}, M) → H²(Q, M) → Hom(H₂(Q), M) → 0 is exact, where the second
      map sends η to h_η; it is natural in M.

By (F1), h_ξ has image C ∩ H′ = C ∩ G = C₀. Let ι : C₀ ↪ C. By (F2) applied to the coefficient group C₀ there
is ξ* ∈ H²(H̄, C₀) with h_{ξ*} = h_ξ (viewed as a map H₂(H̄) → C₀). Let H* be the central extension of H̄ by
C₀ with class ξ*; then |H*| = |H̄| · |C₀|. By naturality h_{ι_*ξ*} = ι∘h_{ξ*} = h_ξ, so ξ − ι_*ξ* has trivial
Hopf map, i.e. lies in Ext(H̄^{ab}, C) ⊆ H²(H̄, C); let A be a central extension of H̄ by C with this class.
By (F1), A′ ∩ C = 1, so A′ → H̄′ is an isomorphism.

The extension ι_*ξ* is the pushout E₁ := (H* × C)/{(c, c^{-1}) : c ∈ C₀} = H* ∘_{C₀} C (central product), and
E₁′ = (H*)′ because C is central in E₁ and E₁ = H*·C.

Now ξ = ι_*ξ* + (ξ − ι_*ξ*) is a Baer sum: H ≅ (E₁ ×_{H̄} A)/Δ, where E₁ ×_{H̄} A is the fibre product over H̄
(a central extension of H̄ by C × C) and Δ = {(c, c^{-1}) : c ∈ C}. Let F := E₁ ×_{H̄} A.

Claim: F′ = E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′ ≅ E₁′.
Indeed F′ ⊆ E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′ := {(x,y) ∈ E₁′ × A′ : x and y have the same image in H̄′}. By naturality of the
Hopf map under the two projections F → E₁, F → A, the Hopf map of F is (h_{ι_*ξ*}, h_{ξ−ι_*ξ*}) = (h_ξ, 0),
whose image is C₀ × 1; by (F1) F′ ∩ (C × C) = C₀ × 1. As F′ maps onto H̄′, |F′| = |H̄′| · |C₀|. On the other
hand |E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′| = Σ_{z ∈ H̄′} |E₁′ ∩ π^{-1}(z)| · |A′ ∩ π^{-1}(z)| = |H̄′| · |E₁′ ∩ C| · |A′ ∩ C| =
|H̄′| · |C₀| · 1. Hence F′ = E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′, and projection to the first coordinate is an isomorphism
E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′ → E₁′ (injective because A′ ∩ C = 1 forces y to be determined by the image of x; surjective
because A′ → H̄′ is onto). This proves the claim.

Finally F′ ∩ Δ = {(c, c^{-1}) : c ∈ C₀, c^{-1} = 1} = 1, so
  H′ = (F/Δ)′ = F′Δ/Δ ≅ F′ ≅ E₁′ = (H*)′.
Therefore (H*)′ ≅ H′ = G, and by (3.2)

  |H*| = |H̄| · |C₀| ≤ |Aut(G)| · e^{2m} · |Z| · |Z|.

This proves Theorem A. ∎

## 5. Remarks on complexity

* The witness H* of Theorem A has order at most |Aut(G)| |Z(G)|² (2 exp Z(G))^{2⌈log₂|G|⌉}. With
  |Aut(G)| ≤ |G|^{log₂|G|} this is |G|^{O(log|G|)}; the property "(H*)′ ≅ G" is verifiable in time
  quasi-polynomial in |G| (group isomorphism for groups of order N is decidable in time N^{O(log N)}). Hence
  the decision problem is in nondeterministic quasi-polynomial time. (The naive deterministic algorithm —
  enumerate all groups up to the bound — is of course far worse.)
* For centerless G, Theorem B gives a much better algorithm: compute A = Aut(G), I = Inn(G), and decide whether
  some subgroup Q with I ≤ Q ≤ A has Q′ = I. Since Q′ = I forces Q/I abelian, one only needs subgroups of
  A/I that are abelian; e.g. it suffices to test the subgroups ⟨I, q₁,…,q_r⟩ with r ≤ 2⌈log₂|G|⌉.
* The necessary condition of Theorem B is not sufficient in general when Z(G) ≠ 1 is possible a priori; the
  brute-force cross-check in `work/p21_32/` compares the criterion with actual derived subgroups for all groups
  G of order ≤ 32 (see the log for the outcome).

# Problem 21.32 (P. J. Cameron) — "Is G the derived subgroup of some finite group?" is decidable

**Problem 21.32.** Is the following problem decidable, and if so, what is its complexity? Given a finite
group G, is there a finite group H such that the derived subgroup of H is isomorphic to G?

**Answer.** Yes, it is decidable. More precisely:

> **Theorem A.** Let G be a finite group, let e = 2·exp(Z(G)), and let m = ⌈log₂|G|⌉. If G ≅ H′ for some
> finite group H, then G ≅ (H*)′ for a finite group H* with
>
>   |H*| ≤ |Aut(G)| · |Z(G)|² · e^{2m}.
>
> Consequently the problem is decidable (search all groups of order at most this bound), and the bound is
> quasi-polynomial in |G| (since |Aut(G)| ≤ |G|^{log₂|G|}); so the problem lies in NTIME(n^{O(log n)}) for
> input size n = |G| (a witness H* of quasi-polynomial size, on which "H*′ ≅ G" is checked in quasi-polynomial
> time).

> **Theorem B (necessary condition; sufficient when Z(G)=1).** If G ≅ H′ for a finite group H, then there is a
> subgroup Q with Inn(G) ≤ Q ≤ Aut(G) and Q′ = Inn(G). If Z(G) = 1 the converse holds: G ≅ H′ for some finite
> H if and only if Inn(G) ≅ G is the derived subgroup of some subgroup Q of Aut(G) containing Inn(G).
> In particular, for centerless G the problem reduces to a finite computation inside Aut(G).

Examples: S₃ and D₈ are not derived subgroups of any finite group (Theorem B: Aut(S₃)=S₃ has derived
subgroup C₃ ≠ Inn(S₃); Aut(D₈) = D₈ has no subgroup Q ⊇ Inn(D₈) ≅ C₂² with Q′ = C₂²), while Q₈ = SL(2,3)′
and A₄ = S₄′. (These examples are confirmed by brute force in `work/p21_32/`.)

## 1. Set-up and the basic structure

Throughout, H is a finite group with H′ = G (we identify G with the subgroup H′ ≤ H). Put

  K := C_H(G),  Z := Z(G).

(1.1) H/G is abelian (as G = H′).
(1.2) K ⊴ H and H/K embeds in Aut(G) (conjugation action). Its image Q := H/K contains Inn(G) = GK/K.
(1.3) K ∩ G = C_G(G) = Z.
(1.4) [H, K] ≤ H′ ∩ K = G ∩ K = Z (using K ⊴ H). In particular K′ ≤ Z, so K is nilpotent of class ≤ 2, and
      K/Z is central in H/Z. Also K ≤ C_H(Z) since K centralises G ⊇ Z.
(1.5) Commutator calculus: for h,h′ ∈ H and k,k′ ∈ K,
        [hk, h′k′] = [h,h′k′]^k [k,h′k′] = ([h,k′][h,h′]^{k′})^k · [k,k′][k,h′]^{k′}.
      The factors [h,k′], [k,h′], [k,k′] lie in Z ≤ K, and Z is centralised by K. Hence, for any subgroup
      H₁ ≤ H with H = H₁K, one has
        G = H′ = H₁′ · [H₁,K] · K′,                                             (∗)
      where the right-hand side is a subgroup because [H₁,K]K′ ≤ Z ≤ G ≤ H₁ normalises H₁′ and H₁′ ≤ G
      is centralised by K.

**Proof of Theorem B.** Put H̃ = H/Z, K̃ = K/Z, G̃ = G/Z. By (1.4) K̃ is central in H̃, and H̃/K̃ ≅ H/K = Q.
Since H′ = G we get H̃′ = G̃, and G̃ ∩ K̃ = (G ∩ K)/Z = 1 by (1.3). The projection π: H̃ → Q maps H̃′ onto
Q′ with kernel H̃′ ∩ K̃ = G̃ ∩ K̃ = 1, so π restricts to an isomorphism G̃ = H̃′ → Q′; but π(G̃) = π(GK/K) is
precisely the group Inn(G) of inner automorphisms. Hence Q′ = Inn(G).
If Z(G) = 1 then K ∩ G = 1, [H,K] = 1, so K ≤ Z(H) and H′ ∩ K = 1; hence H′ ≅ (H/K)′ = Q′ = Inn(G) ≅ G is
realised by the subgroup Q ≤ Aut(G) itself (take H := Q). ∎

## 2. Reduction 1: bounded rank

Since G = H′ is generated by commutators [a,b] (a,b ∈ H) and every generating set of a group of order |G|
contains a generating subset of size ≤ log₂|G|, we can choose a₁,b₁,…,a_m,b_m ∈ H, m ≤ log₂|G|, with
G = ⟨[a_i,b_i] : i ≤ m⟩. Let H₀ := ⟨G, a₁,b₁,…,a_m,b_m⟩. Then H₀′ ⊇ ⟨[a_i,b_i]⟩ = G and H₀′ ≤ H′ = G, so
H₀′ = G. Moreover H₀/G is an abelian group generated by the 2m images of the a_i, b_i.
Replacing H by H₀ we may and do assume:

  (2.1) H′ = G and H/G is abelian, generated by 2m ≤ 2log₂|G| elements.

Then K/Z ≅ KG/G ≤ H/G is abelian and generated by ≤ 2m elements (subgroups of a d-generated finite abelian
group are d-generated).

## 3. Reduction 2: a large central subgroup

Let e := 2·exp(Z). For k,k′ ∈ K we have [k,k′] ∈ K′ ≤ Z (1.4), and K has class ≤ 2, so
(kk′)^e = k^e k′^e [k′,k]^{e(e−1)/2}; since e(e−1)/2 is a multiple of exp(Z) (e is even), the last factor is
trivial. Hence k ↦ k^e is an endomorphism of K and C := K^e = {k^e : k ∈ K} is a characteristic subgroup of K,
so C ⊴ H. For h ∈ H and k ∈ K, [h,k] ∈ Z is centralised by k, so [h,k^e] = [h,k]^e = 1. Thus

  (3.1) C ≤ Z(H).

Furthermore K/C has exponent dividing e, and K/CZ is an abelian group (a quotient of K/Z) generated by ≤ 2m
elements of exponent dividing e, so |K : CZ| ≤ e^{2m} and

  (3.2) |H/C| = |H:K| · |K:CZ| · |CZ:C| ≤ |Aut(G)| · e^{2m} · |Z|.

## 4. Reduction 3: replacing the central subgroup C by C ∩ G (Baer sums)

Put H̄ := H/C and C₀ := C ∩ G = C ∩ Z (a subgroup of Z, as C ≤ K). Since C is central, H is a central
extension 1 → C → H → H̄ → 1 with class ξ ∈ H²(H̄, C) (trivial action). Recall two standard facts for a
central extension 1 → M → E → Q → 1 with class η:

 (F1) (Hopf) The 5-term exact sequence H₂(E) → H₂(Q) → M → E^{ab} → Q^{ab} → 0 shows that the image of the
      "Hopf map" h_η : H₂(Q) → M equals M ∩ E′.
 (F2) (Universal coefficients) 0 → Ext(Q^{ab}, M) → H²(Q, M) → Hom(H₂(Q), M) → 0 is exact, where the second
      map sends η to h_η; it is natural in M.

By (F1), h_ξ has image C ∩ H′ = C ∩ G = C₀. Let ι : C₀ ↪ C. By (F2) applied to the coefficient group C₀ there
is ξ* ∈ H²(H̄, C₀) with h_{ξ*} = h_ξ (viewed as a map H₂(H̄) → C₀). Let H* be the central extension of H̄ by
C₀ with class ξ*; then |H*| = |H̄| · |C₀|. By naturality h_{ι_*ξ*} = ι∘h_{ξ*} = h_ξ, so ξ − ι_*ξ* has trivial
Hopf map, i.e. lies in Ext(H̄^{ab}, C) ⊆ H²(H̄, C); let A be a central extension of H̄ by C with this class.
By (F1), A′ ∩ C = 1, so A′ → H̄′ is an isomorphism.

The extension ι_*ξ* is the pushout E₁ := (H* × C)/{(c, c^{-1}) : c ∈ C₀} = H* ∘_{C₀} C (central product), and
E₁′ = (H*)′ because C is central in E₁ and E₁ = H*·C.

Now ξ = ι_*ξ* + (ξ − ι_*ξ*) is a Baer sum: H ≅ (E₁ ×_{H̄} A)/Δ, where E₁ ×_{H̄} A is the fibre product over H̄
(a central extension of H̄ by C × C) and Δ = {(c, c^{-1}) : c ∈ C}. Let F := E₁ ×_{H̄} A.

Claim: F′ = E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′ ≅ E₁′.
Indeed F′ ⊆ E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′ := {(x,y) ∈ E₁′ × A′ : x and y have the same image in H̄′}. By naturality of the
Hopf map under the two projections F → E₁, F → A, the Hopf map of F is (h_{ι_*ξ*}, h_{ξ−ι_*ξ*}) = (h_ξ, 0),
whose image is C₀ × 1; by (F1) F′ ∩ (C × C) = C₀ × 1. As F′ maps onto H̄′, |F′| = |H̄′| · |C₀|. On the other
hand |E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′| = Σ_{z ∈ H̄′} |E₁′ ∩ π^{-1}(z)| · |A′ ∩ π^{-1}(z)| = |H̄′| · |E₁′ ∩ C| · |A′ ∩ C| =
|H̄′| · |C₀| · 1. Hence F′ = E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′, and projection to the first coordinate is an isomorphism
E₁′ ×_{H̄′} A′ → E₁′ (injective because A′ ∩ C = 1 forces y to be determined by the image of x; surjective
because A′ → H̄′ is onto). This proves the claim.

Finally F′ ∩ Δ = {(c, c^{-1}) : c ∈ C₀, c^{-1} = 1} = 1, so
  H′ = (F/Δ)′ = F′Δ/Δ ≅ F′ ≅ E₁′ = (H*)′.
Therefore (H*)′ ≅ H′ = G, and by (3.2)

  |H*| = |H̄| · |C₀| ≤ |Aut(G)| · e^{2m} · |Z| · |Z|.

This proves Theorem A. ∎

## 5. Remarks on complexity

* The witness H* of Theorem A has order at most |Aut(G)| |Z(G)|² (2 exp Z(G))^{2⌈log₂|G|⌉}. With
  |Aut(G)| ≤ |G|^{log₂|G|} this is |G|^{O(log|G|)}; the property "(H*)′ ≅ G" is verifiable in time
  quasi-polynomial in |G| (group isomorphism for groups of order N is decidable in time N^{O(log N)}). Hence
  the decision problem is in nondeterministic quasi-polynomial time. (The naive deterministic algorithm —
  enumerate all groups up to the bound — is of course far worse.)
* For centerless G, Theorem B gives a much better algorithm: compute A = Aut(G), I = Inn(G), and decide whether
  some subgroup Q with I ≤ Q ≤ A has Q′ = I. Since Q′ = I forces Q/I abelian, one only needs subgroups of
  A/I that are abelian; e.g. it suffices to test the subgroups ⟨I, q₁,…,q_r⟩ with r ≤ 2⌈log₂|G|⌉.
* The necessary condition of Theorem B is not sufficient in general when Z(G) ≠ 1 is possible a priori; the
  brute-force cross-check in `work/p21_32/` compares the criterion with actual derived subgroups for all groups
